450	### Add supporting files
451	
452	Skills can include multiple files in their directory. This keeps `SKILL.md` focused on the essentials while letting Claude access detailed reference material only when needed. Large reference docs, API specifications, or example collections don't need to load into context every time the skill runs.
453	
454	```text theme={null}
455	my-skill/
456	├── SKILL.md (required - overview and navigation)
457	├── reference.md (detailed API docs - loaded when needed)
458	├── examples.md (usage examples - loaded when needed)
459	└── scripts/
460	    └── helper.py (utility script - executed, not loaded)
461	```
462	
463	Reference supporting files from `SKILL.md` so Claude knows what each file contains and when to load it:
464	
465	```markdown theme={null}
466	## Additional resources
467	
468	- For complete API details, see [reference.md](reference.md)
469	- For usage examples, see [examples.md](examples.md)
470	```
471	
472	<Tip>Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files.</Tip>
473	
474	### Control who invokes a skill
475	
476	By default, both you and Claude can invoke any skill. You can type `/skill-name` to invoke it directly, and Claude can load it automatically when relevant to your conversation. Two frontmatter fields let you restrict this:
477	
478	* **`disable-model-invocation: true`**: Only you can invoke the skill. Use this for workflows with side effects or that you want to control timing, like `/commit`, `/deploy`, or `/send-slack-message`. You don't want Claude deciding to deploy because your code looks ready.
479	
480	* **`user-invocable: false`**: Only Claude can invoke the skill. Use this for background knowledge that isn't actionable as a command. A `legacy-system-context` skill explains how an old system works. Claude should know this when relevant, but `/legacy-system-context` isn't a meaningful action for users to take.
481	
482	This example creates a deploy skill that only you can trigger. If you set `disable-model-invocation: true`, Claude can't run the skill automatically:
483	
484	```yaml theme={null}
485	---
486	name: deploy
487	description: Deploy the application to production
488	disable-model-invocation: true
489	---
490	
491	Deploy $ARGUMENTS to production:
492	
493	1. Run the test suite
494	2. Build the application
495	3. Push to the deployment target
496	4. Verify the deployment succeeded
497	```
498	
499	If Claude tries anyway, Claude Code blocks the call and instructs it not to reproduce the deploy steps another way, so expect Claude to suggest running `/deploy` yourself.
500	
501	Here's how the two fields affect invocation and context loading:
502	
503	| Frontmatter                      | You can invoke | Claude can invoke | When loaded into context                                     |
504	| :------------------------------- | :------------- | :---------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
505	| (default)                        | Yes            | Yes               | Description always in context, full skill loads when invoked |
506	| `disable-model-invocation: true` | Yes            | No                | Description not in context, full skill loads when you invoke |
507	| `user-invocable: false`          | No             | Yes               | Description always in context, full skill loads when invoked |
508	
509	<Note>
510	  In a regular session, skill descriptions are loaded into context so Claude knows what's available, but full skill content only loads when invoked. [Subagents with preloaded skills](/docs/en/sub-agents#preload-skills-into-subagents) work differently: the full skill content is injected at startup.
511	</Note>
512	
513	### Skill content lifecycle
514	
515	When you or Claude invoke a skill, the rendered `SKILL.md` content enters the conversation as a single message and stays there across later turns. This persistence applies to the skill's instructions, not its permissions: an [`allowed-tools`](#pre-approve-tools-for-a-skill) grant clears when you send your next message. Claude Code does not re-read the skill file on later turns, so write guidance that should apply throughout a task as standing instructions rather than one-time steps.
516	
517	When Claude re-invokes a skill whose rendered content is identical to the copy already in context, Claude Code adds a short note that the skill is already loaded rather than a second copy of the content. When the rendered content differs, because the arguments changed or a [dynamic context](#inject-dynamic-context) command produced new output, Claude Code appends the full content again.
518	
519	[Auto-compaction](/docs/en/how-claude-code-works#when-context-fills-up) carries invoked skills forward within a token budget. When the conversation is summarized to free context, Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill after the summary, keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each. Re-attached skills share a combined budget of 25,000 tokens. Claude Code fills this budget starting from the most recently invoked skill, so older skills can be dropped entirely after compaction if you have invoked many in one session.
520	
521	If a skill seems to stop influencing behavior after the first response, the content is usually still present and the model is choosing other tools or approaches. Strengthen the skill's `description` and instructions so the model keeps preferring it, or use [hooks](/docs/en/hooks) to enforce behavior deterministically. If the skill is large or you invoked several others after it, re-invoke it after compaction to restore the full content.
522	
523	### Pre-approve tools for a skill
524	
525	The `allowed-tools` field grants permission for the listed tools during the turn that invokes the skill, so Claude can use them without prompting you for approval. The grant clears when you send your next message, even though the skill content [stays in context](#skill-content-lifecycle); invoking the skill again re-applies it for that turn. It does not restrict which tools are available: every tool remains callable, and your [permission settings](/docs/en/permissions) still govern tools that are not listed. To pre-approve tools for the whole session rather than a single turn, add allow rules to those permission settings instead.
526	
527	Workspace trust doesn't gate this field. Claude Code applies a project skill's `allowed-tools` whenever you or Claude invoke the skill, including in a `-p` run in a folder you've never trusted. A skill can grant itself broad tool access, so review the `allowed-tools` of skills checked into a repository before you run Claude Code there.
528	
529	This skill lets Claude run git commands without per-use approval whenever you invoke it:
530	
531	```yaml theme={null}
532	---
533	name: commit
534	description: Stage and commit the current changes
535	disable-model-invocation: true
536	allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *)
537	---
538	```
539	
540	To remove tools from Claude's available pool while a skill is active, list them in `disallowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter. The restriction clears when you send your next message. Like deny rules, the field can't remove [`EndConversation`](/docs/en/tools-reference#endconversation-tool-behavior) while any other tool remains. To block tools across all skills and prompts, add deny rules in your [permission settings](/docs/en/permissions).
541	
542	### Pass arguments to skills
543	
544	Both you and Claude can pass arguments when invoking a skill. Arguments are available via the `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder.
545	
546	This skill fixes a GitHub issue by number. The `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder gets replaced with whatever follows the skill name:
547	
548	```yaml theme={null}
549	---
550	name: fix-issue
551	description: Fix a GitHub issue
552	disable-model-invocation: true
553	---
554	
555	Fix GitHub issue $ARGUMENTS following our coding standards.
556	
557	1. Read the issue description
558	2. Understand the requirements
559	3. Implement the fix
560	4. Write tests
561	5. Create a commit
562	```
563	
564	When you run `/fix-issue 123`, Claude receives "Fix GitHub issue 123 following our coding standards..."
565	
566	If you invoke a skill with arguments but no placeholder in the skill's content receives one, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <your input>` to the end of the skill content so Claude still sees what you typed. A placeholder is `$ARGUMENTS`, an indexed form such as `$1`, or a named argument. An indexed placeholder with no argument at its position stays as literal text and doesn't count as receiving one. A named placeholder counts even when its position has no argument, because it expands to an empty string.
567	
568	You can also stack several skills at the start of one message. Typing `/write-tests /fix-issue 123` loads both skills and passes the trailing text `123` as `$ARGUMENTS` to each of them. Before v2.1.199, only the first skill loaded and received `/fix-issue 123` as literal argument text.
569	
570	Claude Code expands the first skill plus up to five more stacked after it. Expansion stops at the first token that isn't an inline user-invocable skill, so a skill that runs as a [forked subagent](#run-skills-in-a-subagent), such as [`/code-review`](/docs/en/code-review#review-a-diff-locally), or one whose arguments may themselves start with a slash command, such as `/loop`, also ends the run there. That token and everything after it become the argument text for every expanded skill. `/code-review` runs as a forked subagent from v2.1.218; on earlier versions it ran inline and stacked.
571	
572	To access individual arguments by position, use `$ARGUMENTS[N]` or the shorter `$N`:
573	
574	```yaml theme={null}
575	---
576	name: migrate-component
577	description: Migrate a component from one language to another
578	---
579	
580	Migrate the $ARGUMENTS[0] component from $ARGUMENTS[1] to $ARGUMENTS[2].
581	Preserve all existing behavior and tests.
582	```
583	
584	Running `/migrate-component SearchBar JavaScript TypeScript` replaces `$ARGUMENTS[0]` with `SearchBar`, `$ARGUMENTS[1]` with `JavaScript`, and `$ARGUMENTS[2]` with `TypeScript`. The same skill using the `$N` shorthand:
585	
586	```yaml theme={null}
587	---
588	name: migrate-component
589	description: Migrate a component from one language to another
590	---
591	
592	Migrate the $0 component from $1 to $2.
593	Preserve all existing behavior and tests.
594	```
595	
596	## Advanced patterns
597	
598	### Inject dynamic context
599	
600	The `` !`<command>` `` syntax runs shell commands before the skill content is sent to Claude. The command output replaces the placeholder, so Claude receives actual data, not the command itself. Claude Code doesn't run these commands on your machine when the skill is [synced from your claude.ai account](#how-claude-code-handles-the-body-of-a-synced-skill).
601	
602	This skill summarizes a pull request by fetching live PR data with the GitHub CLI. The `` !`gh pr diff` `` and other commands run first, and their output gets inserted into the prompt:
603	
604	```yaml theme={null}
605	---
606	name: pr-summary
607	description: Summarize changes in a pull request
608	context: fork
609	agent: Explore
610	allowed-tools: Bash(gh *)
611	---
612	
613	## Pull request context
614	- PR diff: !`gh pr diff`
615	- PR comments: !`gh pr view --comments`
616	- Changed files: !`gh pr diff --name-only`
617	
618	## Your task
619	Summarize this pull request...
620	```
621	
622	Substitution runs once over the original file. Command output is inserted as plain text and is not re-scanned for further `` !`<command>` `` placeholders, so a command cannot emit a placeholder for a later pass to expand.
623	
624	The inline form is only recognized when `!` appears at the start of a line or immediately after whitespace. If `!` follows another character, as in `` KEY=!`cmd` ``, the placeholder is left as literal text and the command does not run.
625	
626	For multi-line commands, use a fenced code block opened with ` ```! ` instead of the inline form:
627	
628	````markdown theme={null}
629	## Environment
630	```!
631	node --version
632	git status --short
633	```
634	````
635	
636	To disable this behavior for skills and custom commands from user, project, plugin, or [additional-directory](#skills-from-additional-directories) sources, set `"disableSkillShellExecution": true` in [settings](/docs/en/settings). Each command is replaced with `[shell command execution disabled by policy]` instead of being run. Bundled and managed skills are not affected. This setting is most useful in [managed settings](/docs/en/managed-settings), where users cannot override it.
637	
638	Claude Code never runs these commands on your machine when they appear in skills [synced from your claude.ai account](#how-synced-skills-behave), regardless of this setting. [How Claude Code handles the body of a synced skill](#how-claude-code-handles-the-body-of-a-synced-skill) says what Claude receives in place of the command in each kind of session.
639	
640	<Tip>
641	  To request deeper reasoning when a skill runs, include `ultrathink` anywhere in the skill content. See [Use ultrathink for one-off deep reasoning](/docs/en/model-config#use-ultrathink-for-one-off-deep-reasoning).
642	</Tip>
643	
644	#### How injected commands run
645	
646	Claude Code picks the tool that runs a skill's injected commands from the `shell` key in the skill's frontmatter and your environment. Every combination runs the commands through the Bash tool or the PowerShell tool, except one that fails the invocation outright:
647	
648	* `shell: powershell`, with the [PowerShell tool](/docs/en/tools-reference#powershell-tool) enabled: the commands run through the PowerShell tool.
649	* `shell: bash` when bash isn't available: the invocation fails before any command runs. This happens on Windows without Git Bash. Claude Code shows ``Skill <name> requires bash (`shell: bash` in frontmatter) but Git Bash was not found``.
650	* Any other combination: the commands run through the Bash tool when bash is available. When it isn't, they run through the PowerShell tool.
651	
652	Either tool runs the commands the same way it runs Claude's own shell commands. They share the working directory, timeout, and output handling:
653	
654	* **Working directory**: Claude Code runs each command in the session shell's current working directory. That directory moves when Claude runs `cd`. Use [`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` or `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`](#available-string-substitutions) in paths that must resolve the same way every time.
655	* **stderr**: with the default `bash` shell, Claude Code merges stderr into stdout. Anything the command writes to stderr appears in the injected text.
656	* **Timeout**: each command runs under the Bash tool's default 2-minute [timeout](/docs/en/tools-reference#timeout-and-output-limits). When the Bash tool [moves a timed-out command to the background](/docs/en/tools-reference#background-commands), the skill still renders. The injected text reports the move and names the background task and the file collecting the command's output. When the command is one the Bash tool never auto-backgrounds, Claude Code kills it at the timeout. That failure [aborts the invocation](#when-an-injected-command-fails).
657	* **Output size**: output past the Bash tool's inline ceiling arrives as a file path plus a short preview, not truncated text. [Output limits](/docs/en/tools-reference#output-limits) covers the ceiling and which variable adjusts which boundary.
658	
659	The PowerShell tool applies the same timeout, backgrounding, and output-ceiling behavior to the commands it runs. See the [PowerShell tool](/docs/en/tools-reference#powershell-tool) section for its specifics.
660	
661	#### When an injected command fails
662	
663	A failed command aborts the entire skill invocation, not just its own placeholder. Claude never sees the skill content for that invocation. The abort shows `Shell command failed for pattern "..."`. The error message includes the command's output under `[stderr]`.
664	
665	With the default `bash` shell, any non-zero exit code counts as a failure. One carveout applies: Claude Code treats exit code 1 from [search and comparison commands](/docs/en/tools-reference#output-limits) as a normal result and injects their output. Exit codes of 2 or higher fail even for those commands.
666	
667	Which commands get the carveout depends on the shell:
668	
669	* Default `bash` shell: the commands listed under [Output limits](/docs/en/tools-reference#output-limits)
670	* `shell: powershell`, when the PowerShell tool is enabled: a [different set](/docs/en/tools-reference#shell-selection-in-settings-hooks-and-skills) that includes `grep` and `git diff` but not `find` or `diff`
671	
672	With the default `bash` shell, append `|| true` to any other command you expect to exit non-zero. A check script that exits 1 when it finds problems is one example.
673	
674	Injected commands never prompt for permission. When a command's permission check returns anything other than allow, Claude Code aborts the invocation. This includes a rule that would normally ask you. The abort shows `Shell command permission check failed for pattern "..."`.
675	
676	To keep an unmatched command from aborting here, pre-approve it with [`allowed-tools`](#pre-approve-tools-for-a-skill). A matching ask or deny rule still aborts the invocation regardless of `allowed-tools`. See [Manage permissions](/docs/en/permissions#manage-permissions).
677	
678	### Run skills in a subagent
679	
680	Add `context: fork` to your frontmatter when you want a skill to run in isolation. The skill content becomes the prompt that drives the subagent. It won't have access to your conversation history.
681	
682	The forked subagent runs in the [background](/docs/en/sub-agents#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background): you keep working while it runs, and its result arrives in your conversation when it completes. Set `background: false` in the frontmatter to instead wait for the result in the turn that invoked the skill. Before v2.1.218, forked skills always blocked the turn until they finished.
683	
684	Claude Code also waits for the result, even when the skill doesn't set `background: false`, in cases like these:
685	
686	* In non-interactive mode, with the `-p` flag or the Agent SDK
687	* When you set [`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS`](/docs/en/env-vars) to `1`, which also turns off all other background task features
688	* When you invoke a forked skill while an earlier invocation of the same skill is still running
689	* When a [scheduled task](/docs/en/scheduled-tasks) fires with the skill as its prompt
690	
691	A backgrounded fork also runs with the [narrower tool set that applies to background subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background): the skill's subagent is a regular agent type, so the exemption for subagents that fork the conversation doesn't cover it. If your skill's steps depend on a tool outside that set, set `background: false` to keep the full tool set.
692	
693	A forked skill that runs in the background applies its edits outside your session's [checkpoints](/docs/en/checkpointing), so `/rewind` doesn't undo them; use git to revert them.
694	
695	<Warning>
696	  `context: fork` only makes sense for skills with explicit instructions. If your skill contains guidelines like "use these API conventions" without a task, the subagent receives the guidelines but no actionable prompt, and returns without meaningful output.
697	</Warning>
698	
699	Skills and [subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents) work together in two directions:
700	
701	| Approach                     | System prompt            | Task                        | Also loads                                          |
702	| :--------------------------- | :----------------------- | :-------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- |
703	| Skill with `context: fork`   | From agent type          | SKILL.md content            | CLAUDE.md, except when the agent is Explore or Plan |
704	| Subagent with `skills` field | Subagent's markdown body | Claude's delegation message | Preloaded skills + CLAUDE.md                        |
705	
706	With `context: fork`, you write the task in your skill and pick an agent type to execute it. The built-in Explore and Plan agents [skip CLAUDE.md and git status](/docs/en/sub-agents#what-loads-at-startup) to keep their context small, so a forked skill using `agent: Explore` sees only the SKILL.md content and the agent's own system prompt. For the inverse, where you define a custom subagent that uses skills as reference material, see [Subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents#preload-skills-into-subagents).
707	
708	#### Example: Research skill using Explore agent
709	
710	This skill runs research in a forked Explore agent. The skill content becomes the task, and the agent provides read-only tools optimized for codebase exploration:
711	
712	```yaml theme={null}
713	---
714	name: deep-research
715	description: Research a topic thoroughly
716	context: fork
717	agent: Explore
718	---
719	
720	Research $ARGUMENTS thoroughly:
721	
722	1. Find relevant files using Glob and Grep
723	2. Read and analyze the code
724	3. Summarize findings with specific file references
725	```
726	
727	When this skill runs:
728	
729	1. A new isolated context is created
730	2. The subagent receives the skill content as its prompt ("Research \$ARGUMENTS thoroughly...")
731	3. The `agent` field determines the execution environment (model, tools, and permissions)
732	4. The subagent summarizes its results and returns them to your main conversation when it finishes
733	
734	The `agent` field specifies which subagent configuration to use. Options include built-in agents (`Explore`, `Plan`, `general-purpose`) or any custom subagent from `.claude/agents/`. If omitted, uses `general-purpose`.
735	
736	### Restrict Claude's skill access
737	
738	By default, Claude can invoke any skill that doesn't have `disable-model-invocation: true` set. Skills that define `allowed-tools` grant Claude access to those tools without per-use approval during the turn that invokes the skill; the grant clears when you send your next message. Your [permission settings](/docs/en/permissions) still govern baseline approval behavior for all other tools. A few built-in commands are also available through the Skill tool, including `/init` and `/security-review`. Other built-in commands such as `/compact` are not.
739	
740	Three ways to control which skills Claude can invoke:
741	
742	**Disable all skills** by denying the Skill tool in `/permissions`:
743	
744	```text theme={null}
745	# Add to deny rules:
746	Skill
747	```
748	
749	**Allow or deny specific skills** using [permission rules](/docs/en/permissions):
750	
751	```text theme={null}
752	# Allow only specific skills
753	Skill(commit)
754	Skill(review-pr *)
755	
756	# Deny specific skills
757	Skill(deploy *)
758	```
759	
760	Permission syntax: `Skill(name)` for exact match, `Skill(name *)` for prefix match with any arguments.
761	
762	**Hide individual skills** by adding `disable-model-invocation: true` to their frontmatter. This removes the skill from Claude's context entirely.
763	
764	<Note>
765	  With `user-invocable: false`, you can't invoke the skill, but Claude still can. To keep Claude from invoking it through the Skill tool, set `disable-model-invocation: true`.
766	</Note>
767	
768	### Override skill visibility from settings
769	
770	The `skillOverrides` setting controls skill visibility from your [settings](/docs/en/settings) instead of the skill's own frontmatter. Use it for skills whose SKILL.md you don't want to edit, such as ones checked into a shared project repo. The `/skills` menu writes it for you: highlight a skill and press `Space` to cycle states, then `Esc` to save to `.claude/settings.local.json`.
771	
772	Each key is a skill name and each value is one of four states:
773	
774	| Value                   | Listed to Claude     | In `/` menu |
775	| :---------------------- | :------------------- | :---------- |
776	| `"on"`                  | Name and description | Yes         |
777	| `"name-only"`           | Name only            | Yes         |
778	| `"user-invocable-only"` | Hidden               | Yes         |
779	| `"off"`                 | Hidden               | Hidden      |
780	
781	The `/skills` menu labels the `"user-invocable-only"` state `user-only`.
782	
783	As of v2.1.199, `"off"` also hides the skill from the command lists advertised to [Remote Control](/docs/en/remote-control) clients and to [Agent SDK](/docs/en/agent-sdk/skills#discover-available-commands) callers, in addition to the terminal `/` menu. Invoking a hidden skill by its full name still returns the `skillOverrides` error instead of running it.
784	
785	A skill that is absent from `skillOverrides` is treated as `"on"`. The example below collapses one skill to its name and turns another off entirely:
786	
787	```json theme={null}
788	{
789	  "skillOverrides": {
790	    "legacy-context": "name-only",
791	    "deploy": "off"
792	  }
793	}
794	```
795	
796	Plugin skills are not affected by `skillOverrides`. Manage those through `/plugin` instead.
797	
798	## Evaluate and iterate on a skill
799	
800	Seeing a skill trigger tells you Claude found it, not that it did what you intended. To know a skill is working, measure two things separately: whether Claude invokes it on the prompts it should, and whether the output matches what you expect when it does.
801	
802	The check for both is a baseline comparison. Collect a few realistic prompts, run each one in a fresh session with the skill available and again with it [disabled](#override-skill-visibility-from-settings), and compare the results. A fresh session matters because leftover context from authoring the skill will mask gaps in the written instructions.
803	
804	### Run evals with skill-creator
805	
806	The [`skill-creator` plugin](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/plugins/skill-creator) automates the comparison loop inside Claude Code. Install it from the official marketplace:
807	
808	```text theme={null}
809	/plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official
810	```
811	
812	If the install fails, match the message Claude Code reports:
813	
814	* `Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found`: add the marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official`, then retry the install.
815	* The plugin is [not found in the marketplace](/docs/en/discover-plugins#install-plugins): check the plugin name.
816	
817	If the install summary reports `Run /reload-plugins to activate.`, run that command to make the plugin's skills available in the current session. Then ask Claude to evaluate an existing skill, for example `evaluate my summarize-changes skill with skill-creator`. The plugin walks you through writing test cases and runs the loop:
818	
819	* **Test cases**: stores prompts, input files, and expected behavior in `evals/evals.json` inside the skill directory
820	* **Isolated runs**: spawns a [subagent](/docs/en/sub-agents) per test case so each run starts with a clean context, and records token count and duration
821	* **Grading**: checks each assertion against the output and writes pass or fail with evidence to `grading.json`
822	* **Benchmark**: aggregates pass rate, time, and tokens for with-skill versus without-skill into `benchmark.json` so you can compare the pass-rate improvement against the token and time overhead
823	* **Version comparison**: runs a blind A/B between two versions of the skill so you can confirm an edit is an improvement before committing it
824	* **Description tuning**: generates should-trigger and should-not-trigger prompts, measures the hit rate, and proposes description edits when the skill activates on the wrong requests
825	* **Review viewer**: opens an HTML report where you inspect each output and record qualitative feedback that the next iteration reads
826	
827	For the eval file format and the full iteration workflow, see [Evaluating skill output quality](https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/evaluating-skills) on agentskills.io. For background on the benchmark and comparison modes, see the [skill-creator announcement](https://claude.com/blog/improving-skill-creator-test-measure-and-refine-agent-skills).
828	
829	## Share skills
830	
831	Skills can be distributed at different scopes depending on your audience:
832	
833	* **Project skills**: Commit `.claude/skills/` to version control
834	* **Plugins**: Create a `skills/` directory in your [plugin](/docs/en/plugins)
835	* **Managed**: Deploy organization-wide through [managed settings](/docs/en/managed-settings)
836	
837	### Generate visual output
838	
839	Skills can bundle and run scripts in any language, giving Claude capabilities beyond what's possible in a single prompt. One pattern is generating visual output: interactive HTML files that open in your browser for exploring data, debugging, or creating reports.
840	
841	This example creates a codebase explorer: an interactive tree view where you can expand and collapse directories, see file sizes at a glance, and identify file types by color.
842	
843	Create the Skill directory:
844	
845	```bash theme={null}
846	mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/codebase-visualizer/scripts
847	```
848	
849	Save this to `~/.claude/skills/codebase-visualizer/SKILL.md`. The description tells Claude when to activate this Skill, and the instructions tell Claude to run the bundled script. The script path uses [`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`](#available-string-substitutions) so it resolves correctly whether the skill is installed at the personal, project, or plugin level:
850	
851	````yaml theme={null}
852	---
853	name: codebase-visualizer
854	description: Generate an interactive collapsible tree visualization of your codebase. Use when exploring a new repo, understanding project structure, or identifying large files.
855	allowed-tools: Bash(python3 *)
856	---
857	
858	# Codebase Visualizer
859	
860	Generate an interactive HTML tree view that shows your project's file structure with collapsible directories.
861	
862	## Usage
863	
864	Run the visualization script from your project root:
865	
866	```bash
867	python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/visualize.py .
868	```
869	
870	This creates `codebase-map.html` in the current directory and opens it in your default browser.
871	
872	## What the visualization shows
873	
874	- **Collapsible directories**: Click folders to expand/collapse
875	- **File sizes**: Displayed next to each file
876	- **Colors**: Different colors for different file types
877	- **Directory totals**: Shows aggregate size of each folder
878	````
879	
880	Save this to `~/.claude/skills/codebase-visualizer/scripts/visualize.py`. This script scans a directory tree and generates a self-contained HTML file with:

883	* A **bar chart** breaking down the codebase by file type (top 8 by size)

1027	
1028	## Troubleshooting
1029	
1030	### Skill not triggering
1031	
1032	If Claude doesn't use your skill when expected:
1033	
1034	1. Check the description includes keywords users would naturally say
1035	2. Verify the skill appears in `What skills are available?`
1036	3. Try rephrasing your request to match the description more closely
1037	4. Invoke it directly with `/skill-name` if the skill is user-invocable
1038	
1039	If the frontmatter YAML is malformed, Claude Code loads the skill body with empty metadata, so `/skill-name` still works but Claude has no `description` to match against. Run with `--debug` to see the parse error.
1040	
1041	To find `SKILL.md` files whose frontmatter doesn't parse, run [`claude plugin validate`](/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces#validate-a-plugin-or-a-directory-without-a-manifest) on the skills directory, for example `claude plugin validate .claude/skills` for project skills or `claude plugin validate ~/.claude/skills` for personal skills. Requires Claude Code v2.1.233 or later.
1042	
1043	### Skill triggers too often
1044	
1045	If Claude uses your skill when you don't want it:
1046	
1047	1. Make the description more specific
1048	2. Add `disable-model-invocation: true` if you only want manual invocation
1049	
1050	### Skill descriptions are cut short
1051	
1052	Claude Code loads a listing of skill names and descriptions into context so Claude knows what's available. The listing always contains every skill name, but if you have many skills, Claude Code shortens descriptions to fit the listing's character budget, which can strip the keywords Claude needs to match your request. The budget scales at 1% of the model's context window. When the listing overflows, Claude Code drops descriptions starting with the skills you invoke least, so the skills you use most keep their full text.
1053	
1054	Run `/doctor` for an estimate of the listing's context cost and its biggest contributors. When the listing exceeds its budget, Claude Code also writes a warning to the debug log, visible with [`--debug`](/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags).
1055	
1056	The Skills row in `/context` reports the size of the listing after the budget is applied, so it matches what the model receives. Before v2.1.196, the row counted the full text of every description and could show a value several times larger than the configured budget.
1057	
1058	To raise the budget, set the [`skillListingBudgetFraction`](/docs/en/settings-reference#skilllistingbudgetfraction) setting (e.g. `0.02` = 2%) or the `SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET` environment variable to a fixed character count. To free budget for other skills, set low-priority entries to `"name-only"` in [`skillOverrides`](#override-skill-visibility-from-settings) so they list without a description. You can also trim the `description` and `when_to_use` text at the source: put the key use case first, since each entry's combined text is capped at 1,536 characters regardless of budget. The cap is configurable with [`skillListingMaxDescChars`](/docs/en/settings-reference#skilllistingmaxdescchars).

# Linter#verifyAndFix Information

Based on the documentation provided, there is **no mention of the number of passes** that the fixing loop performs in the `Linter#verifyAndFix()` section.

The documentation states:

> "This method is similar to verify except that it also runs autofixing logic, similar to the `--fix` flag on the command line."

However, it does not specify how many times the fixing loop repeats or if there is a maximum number of passes. The documentation only describes the method's behavior and output format, without detailing the internal fixing iteration mechanism.

Based on the document provided, here are the verbatim quotes requested:

**(a) On ":exit" selectors and traversal direction:**

"If a key is a node type or a selector plus `:exit`, ESLint calls that **visitor** function while going **up** the tree."

The document also states: "If a key is a node type or a selector, ESLint calls that **visitor** function while going **down** the tree."

**(b) On storing state in create() closure and reporting at Program:exit:**

The document does not contain explicit guidance on this practice.

**(c) On rules running one file at a time with no access to other files:**

The document does not include any statement about rules processing one file at a time or lacking access to other files.

**(d) On fixes being applied in multiple passes:**

"After applying fixes, ESLint will run all the enabled rules again on the fixed code, potentially applying more fixes. This process will repeat up to 10 times, or until no more fixable problems are found."

## What to look for — the check-the-world test

For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**

- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.

**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.

**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)

**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.

**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.

The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

## How to convert one

Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:

> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.

1. **Author the check** in the owning pack, at the ladder's highest check rung the rule allows: an entry
   in `<pack>/declared-checks.json` when its logic is patterns over files, dropping to `<pack>/<rule>.mjs`
   listed in `pack.mjs` only when it needs what patterns can't say. Either way the failure message *is*
   the rule (what / why / fix — plus, for a rule module, the `doc:` pointer back to the prose; a
   declaration carries no pointer and must state its own case).
2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
   doesn't ship.
3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
   - **Declare `since: '<today>'` beside the severity.** A blocking check is enforced as advisory for
     its first two weeks, so a conversion whose backlog the tree still carries lands at its real
     severity now and starts biting once somebody has had time to clear it. Never soften a real
     defect to `advisory` for that reason — the window is what makes softening unnecessary.
   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
   how you decide which paragraphs those are.

**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
check to the same fixture bar.

**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.

When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

## Coming out: the deletion test

Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.

Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
carries.

The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.

Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
**reader**, not mechanized.

## Bounds

- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
  *landed* check now enforces.
- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

# Typed Linting Explanation

Here's what typed linting involves based on the documentation:

"Some typescript-eslint rules utilize TypeScript's type checking APIs to provide much deeper insights into your code. This requires TypeScript to analyze your entire project instead of just the file being linted."

The key enabler is the `parserOptions.projectService: true` setting, which directs the parser to request type information from TypeScript's service for each source file, allowing rules to access type data across the entire codebase.

However, there's a performance consideration: "By using typed linting in your config, you incur the performance penalty of asking TypeScript to do a build of your project before ESLint can do its linting." While small projects may experience negligible slowdowns, larger projects can see noticeably longer lint times as a tradeoff for the enhanced analysis capabilities.

# CodeQL Database and Query Process

According to the documentation, CodeQL's analysis workflow operates through three key phases:

"To create a database, CodeQL first extracts a single relational representation of each source file in the codebase." Following this extraction, "all the data required for analysis (relational data, copied source files, and a language-specific database schema) is imported into a single directory, known as a CodeQL database."

Once the database exists, "one or more queries are executed against it. CodeQL queries are written in a specially-designed object-oriented query language called QL." The documentation emphasizes that you can execute these queries using either the VS Code extension or the CLI.

Finally, the system transforms raw query outputs into actionable findings. "The final step converts results produced during query execution into a form that is more meaningful in the context of the source code," with results displayed through various formats depending on the tool used.

content.content:
# Predicates in QL

**What a predicate is:**

"Strictly speaking, a predicate evaluates to a set of tuples." The document explains that predicates describe logical relations in a QL program, with each predicate containing tuples of uniform length.

**Reusability:**

The content indicates that predicates can be called within other predicates and queries. Built-in predicates are available for use "in any queries without needing to import any additional modules," and custom predicates defined by users function similarly throughout a program.

**Recursive predicates:**

"A predicate in QL can be recursive. This means that it depends, directly or indirectly, on itself." The documentation provides an example using `getANeighbor` that calls itself to create symmetric neighbor relationships, demonstrating how recursion expands predicate results iteratively.

**Least fixed point semantics:**

The provided text does not contain explicit discussion of least fixed point semantics or phrasing like "until no new tuples" regarding recursive predicate evaluation.

# QL Recursive Predicate Evaluation

**Least Fixed Point:**
"To evaluate a recursive predicate, the QL compiler finds the least fixed point of the recursion. In particular, it starts with the empty set of values, and finds new values by repeatedly applying the predicate until the set of values no longer changes."

**Monotonicity Requirement:**
"A valid recursive predicate must also be monotonic. This means that (mutual) recursion is only allowed under an even number of negations."

**Non-Monotonic Recursion Error:**
The documentation explains that recursion under an odd number of negations creates paradoxical situations where "there is no solution to the recursion," using the example of a predicate that holds "precisely when it doesn't hold."

**Base Case Necessity:**
"A valid recursive definition must have a starting point or base case. If a recursive predicate evaluates to the empty set of values, there is usually something wrong."

# Utility Rules in ast-grep

Utility rules enable reusable pattern matching across configurations. The system supports two approaches:

## Local vs Global Utility Rules

**Local utility rules** are defined in a rule file's `utils` field and only available within that file. **Global utility rules** live in a dedicated `utilDirs` directory and work across all project rules.

As the documentation states: "Local utility rules are only available in the config file where they are defined." Conversely, global rules require proper project structure with designated utility directories.

## Using the `matches` Keyword

Rules reference utilities through the `matches` composite rule:

```yaml
utils:
  is-literal:
    any:
      - kind: 'false'
      - kind: number
      - kind: string

rule:
  matches: is-literal
```

## Recursive Patterns

The guide notes that "you can use a utility rule inside another utility" enabling recursive matching. However, there's a critical constraint: "Rule cannot have a cyclic dependency when using `matches`."

Self-referencing is permitted in relational operators like `has` or `inside`, but not in composite `matches` references, preventing infinite recursion loops during AST traversal.

# ast-grep Design Constraints and Analysis Limitations

## No Cross-File Analysis and Type Resolution

From the document:

> "There is no cross-file analysis and no type resolution. `outline` does not resolve imports, follow references, construct call graphs, infer receiver types, or guess that two symbols must be related because they share the same name."

## Three Core Design Constraints

The document identifies these intentional design choices:

1. **Parse on demand**: "Parse current files on demand" rather than maintaining a pre-built index

2. **Stay local**: The tool deliberately avoids "pretending to know global semantics" and keeps operations within individual files

# EarlyLintPass vs LateLintPass

## Access and Timing

**EarlyLintPass:** "works only on the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) level" and operates "after expansion, before lowering to HIR." It lacks access to type and symbol information.

**LateLintPass:** Provides "type information" and includes methods like `maybe_typeck_results` and `typeck_results` that don't exist in the early context.

## When to Choose Each

**EarlyLintPass:** Use when "the lint only deals with syntax-related issues" and doesn't require type information. It's faster and suitable for lints checking function names or grammatical correctness.

**LateLintPass:** Choose when you need type-checking capabilities or must inspect nodes beyond their AST position. The document notes "almost every lint is implemented in a `LateLintPass`" because most lints require checking both syntactic and type information.

## Note on Methods

The document doesn't detail specific `check_*`, `check_crate`, or `check_crate_post` methods. It references that both traits have methods utilizing their respective context types, but doesn't elaborate on particular method signatures or their purposes.

1	# research-project — running an algorithm against ground truth
2	
3	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
4	
5	For every substantive algorithmic change, in this order:
6	
7	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
8	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
9	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
10	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
11	   it** — do not guess.
12	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
13	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
14	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
15	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
16	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
17	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
18	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
19	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
20	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
21	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
22	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
23	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
24	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
25	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
26	
27	### Show, don't just tell
28	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
29	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
30	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
31	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
32	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
33	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
34	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
35	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
36	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
37	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
38	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
39	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
40	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
41	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
42	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
43	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
44	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
45	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
46	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
47	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
48	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
49	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
50	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
51	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
52	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
53	  trustworthy.
54	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
55	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
56	
57	### Interaction cadence
58	- **Keep the owner in the loop with pictures**, proactively, and ask a question only when a
59	  decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — never to confirm work you can
60	  verify yourself.
61	- **Finishing a unit of work** — leave it committed and pushed, so it can be reviewed or
62	  resumed from a fresh session.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
67	
68	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
69	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
70	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
71	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
72	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
73	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
74	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
75	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
76	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
77	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
78	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
79	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
80	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
81	  loudly.
82	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
83	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
84	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
85	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
86	  are requirements, not incidental.
87	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
88	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
89	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
90	  the review overlays.
91	
92	---
93	
94	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
95	
96	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
97	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
98	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
99	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
100	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
101	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
102	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
103	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
104	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
105	  in scope.
106	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
107	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
108	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
109	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
110	
111	---
112	
113	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
114	
115	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
116	if it improves a metric.
117	
118	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
119	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
120	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
121	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
122	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
123	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
124	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
125	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
126	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
127	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
128	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
129	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
130	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
131	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
132	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
133	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
134	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
135	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
136	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
137	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
138	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
139	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
140	
141	---
142	
143	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
144	
145	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
146	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
147	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
148	
149	An iteration note captures:
150	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
151	  showed it).
152	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
153	  possible).
154	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
155	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
156	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
157	
158	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
159	
160	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
161	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
162	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
163	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
164	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
165	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
166	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
167	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
168	
169	### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration
170	
171	When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
172	sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
173	different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —
174	a density, a ratio, a per-unit rate — never the raw number, and never a mean
175	spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,
176	subject or protocol changes *what* is measured, not just how much of it fits in
177	frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.
178	
179	The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
180	off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
181	neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
182	calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
183	input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
184	mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
185	and leave it visible as a known gap.
186	
187	### Definition of done for an accepted change
188	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
189	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
190	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
191	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
192	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
193	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
194	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
195	  changed**.
196	
197	---
198	
199	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
200	
201	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
202	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
203	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
204	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
205	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
206	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
207	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
208	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
209	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
210	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
215	
216	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
217	
218	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
219	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
220	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
221	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
222	- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
223	  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
224	  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
225	  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
226	  until someone re-opens the source.
227	- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
228	  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
229	  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
230	  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
231	  a stated gap is part of that.
232	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
233	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
234	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
235	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
236	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
237	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
238	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
239	
240	---
241	
242	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
243	
244	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
245	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
246	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
247	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
248	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
249	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
250	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
251	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
252	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
253	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
254	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
255	
256	---
257	
258	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
259	
260	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
261	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
262	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
263	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
264	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
265	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
266	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
267	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
268	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
269	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
270	    nothing finer.
271	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
272	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
273	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
274	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
275	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
276	  covered.
277	
278	---
279	
280	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
281	
282	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
283	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
284	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
285	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
286	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
287	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
288	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
289	  exhausted first.
290	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
291	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
292	  warm-up doc.
293	
294	---
295	
296	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
297	
298	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
299	first-class experiments:
300	
301	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
302	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
303	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
304	  couldn't.
305	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
306	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
307	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
308	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
309	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
310	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
311	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
312	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
313	  the very structure you are measuring. (1)
314	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
315	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
316	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
317	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
318	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
319	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
320	
321	---
322	
323	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
324	
325	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
326	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
327	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
328	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
329	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
330	substantially change a sub-step.
331	
332	---
333	
334	## 13. Continuity across sessions
335	
336	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
337	**resumable** state.
338	
339	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
340	  clean checkout.
341	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
342	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
343	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
344	  codebase.
345	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
346	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
347	  metrics current in it.
348	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
349	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
350	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
351	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
352	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
353	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
354	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
355	  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
356	  isn't captured yet.
357	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
358	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
359	
360	---
361	
362	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
363	
364	Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
365	Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
366	such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
367	revived session:
368	
369	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
370	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
371	> the research task itself.**
372	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
