1	# web-scraping — taking data from a site you don't own
2	
3	## Finding the data surface
4	
5	- **Adding a source, or deciding what to parse** — scraping rendered markup is the **last**
6	  resort. Prefer, in order: the hydration blob a server-rendered app embeds in the page, then
7	  the JSON/GraphQL endpoint a single-page app fetches its rows from, and only then the markup
8	  — where you prefer the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD, `og:` tags) over element
9	  positions, because metadata survives a redesign and `.results > div:nth-child(2)` does not.
10	  Finding that surface on a new site is a one-off reconnaissance job with its own procedure,
11	  the [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) skill.
12	
13	- **A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record** — rendered output is **not
14	  deterministic**, so treat the shift the way you'd treat a markup change: re-review it, don't
15	  assume a regression.
16	
17	- **Learning something non-obvious by probing the service** — write it down in a reference doc
18	  beside the scripts: endpoints, auth, the field surface, the enum values. Keep it complete
19	  enough that **nothing needs to re-probe the live service to answer a question**. The
20	  expensive part of this work is the knowledge rather than the code, and re-probing is slow,
21	  rate-limited, sometimes blocked, and occasionally the thing that gets you banned.
22	
23	## Fetching
24	
25	- **Writing the fetch itself** — browser-like headers, a randomized delay between requests, and
26	  exponential backoff on retry. Route **all** outbound page/API fetching through a single
27	  module, so swapping the vendor, the proxy or the credential is one edit with one place to
28	  test.
29	
30	- **Deciding whether to retry a failed request** — retry only what can improve. A gateway or
31	  proxy failure (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) is worth another attempt; any other 4xx is about
32	  your request and will answer the same way forever.
33	
34	- **Porting a fetch to a language-level HTTP client** — carry the retry policy across the
35	  rewrite. `curl --retry` covers exactly that status set and the port silently drops all of it,
36	  so the first transient 500 the old command would have ridden out kills the run.
37	
38	- **Setting the retry budget** — attempts times per-attempt timeout, plus the waits, must fit
39	  inside whatever hard limit kills the process, and the backoff should be injectable so tests
40	  exercise the retry path without sleeping through it.
41	
42	- **One item in a batch failing to fetch** — record and continue. Log the reason per item and
43	  emit a report; one unfetchable item should not abandon the batch.
44	
45	- **A sandbox refusing the target host** — an agent sandbox is commonly **bot-blocked**, and its
46	  egress proxy may refuse the host outright. That refusal is policy: **do not route around it**,
47	  not with a local fetch and not with an ad-hoc workflow spun up to reach the host. Give the
48	  fetch one sanctioned home — a scheduled job or workflow on a runner, with the credential in
49	  repository secrets — and let sessions read the committed raw records instead.
50	
51	- **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** — a 403/400 or a CAPTCHA wall from a
52	  runner or a sandbox is usually the *datacenter IP* being blocked, not the headers, so tuning
53	  them is wasted work. **Reaching a commercial rendering proxy** is the standard answer: a
54	  residential lane clears the IP block, and these services usually execute JavaScript too, so a
55	  single-page app records real content. Ask it to render, and give it a wait-for-selector when
56	  the content you want arrives late. A target that stays blocked even through the proxy is
57	  un-cacheable: say so and stop, rather than hunting for another route.
58	
59	- **Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint** — no bulk endpoint is not the same
60	  as no bulk request. GraphQL lets one document alias the same field many times, and many REST
61	  APIs accept a multi-id parameter. The cap is usually undocumented, so **halve a rejected batch
62	  and retry** — that keeps batch size a throughput knob and never an accuracy one.
63	
64	- **A fetch that cannot produce a page at all** — a bot wall, a dead URL, an empty render is a
65	  dead end, not a pipeline failure: mark the item for a human and **exit successfully**. Failing
66	  the run converges on the same human signal while also implying the pipeline broke, when in
67	  fact it correctly declined. The rest of the batch should still land.
68	
69	## Reading what came back
70	
71	- **Deciding whether a fetch succeeded** — a 200 is not success. An anti-bot interstitial arrives
72	  as a normal-looking 200 (or a 403/503) whose body is a challenge page, and caching it stores
73	  garbage that looks like data. Match the known markers in the first few KB and report it as a
74	  distinct failure reason.
75	
76	- **Getting an empty body back** — nothing rendered. Treat it as a failure of that fetch rather
77	  than as an empty result, and don't retry it: a successful-but-empty response will keep being
78	  successful and empty.
79	
80	- **Choosing which field to read** — prefer the authoritative status enum over the summarizing
81	  convenience boolean, which is routinely wrong: an item can report "not sold out" while its
82	  status says there is nothing left to sell. Take the enum's legal values from the service's own
83	  options endpoint rather than from what you happened to see.
84	
85	- **Filtering rows by a status** — deny-list the bad statuses, don't allow-list the good ones,
86	  and log the set actually observed. A new status then defaults to usable and shows up in your
87	  logs, instead of silently dropping rows.
88	
89	- **Reading a numeric field** — numbers may arrive as strings. Parse; don't assume the JSON type.
90	
91	- **Reducing a set to its "cheapest" or "first"** — that value can be a special case rather than
92	  a value. Filter to what the field means before you reduce over it: a zero-priced accessibility
93	  companion band makes the cheapest ticket for every show free.
94	
95	## Normalizing what you read
96	
97	- **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** — instants usually arrive in UTC while
98	  your domain thinks in local wall-clock. Do the conversion in one function at the ingestion
99	  boundary and have everything downstream speak local time. Slicing digits out of the string
100	  files everything an hour off during daylight saving, and **the result looks completely
101	  plausible** — nothing throws, nothing is empty, the data is simply wrong. Because the failure
102	  is silent, keep a **known-answer probe**: an item whose correct value you know independently
103	  (something named after its own time, a figure published elsewhere), checked after every fresh
104	  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
105	  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.
106	
107	- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
108	  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
109	  survives review.
110	
111	- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
112	  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
113	  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
114	  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
115	  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
116	  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
117	  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
118	  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
119	  about the place.
120	
121	- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
122	  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
123	  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
124	  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
125	  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.
126	
127	- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
128	  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
129	  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
130	  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.
131	
132	## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes
133	
134	- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
135	  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
136	  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
137	  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth. That
138	  split buys three things at once: re-deriving your normalized output becomes an **offline**
139	  operation, so a parser change costs no requests; the committed record doubles as the fixture
140	  for a self-test of the transform that needs no network; and a field you didn't parse this
141	  month is still there next month, because you kept the whole object rather than the subset you
142	  needed at the time.
143	
144	- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
145	  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
146	  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
147	  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
148	  matters.
149	
150	- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
151	  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
152	  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
153	  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
154	  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.
155	
156	- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
157	  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
158	  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
159	  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.
160

1	# Headless browser
2	
3	## Getting a browser
4	
5	- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
6	  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
7	  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
8	  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
9	  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
10	  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
11	  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
12	  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.
13	
14	- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
15	  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
16	  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
17	  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. A reinstall run from the
18	  repo root instead of a scratchpad can dodge that failure outright (a version happens to
19	  resolve that works) and still cost you: it dirties the tracked `package.json`, its lockfile and
20	  `node_modules`, which then need a manual revert before anything can be committed. Resolve the
21	  already-installed package by its global path instead of adding a second copy, at any depth in
22	  the tree.
23	
24	- **When a page depends on a third-party library loaded from a CDN you have not vendored,
25	  stub the library's own API surface rather than trying to make the CDN reachable.** A default
26	  network abort (above) leaves the page's global for that library undefined, so every call into
27	  it throws and the render comes back empty — indistinguishable from a product bug unless you
28	  know the cause. Grep the code under test for the handful of calls it actually makes (a mapping
29	  or charting library often boils down to a handful of constructors and methods) and install a
30	  minimal no-op implementation of just those as an init script, before the page's own scripts run.
31	
32	- **A committed pixel golden is only comparable under the exact build that rendered it.** Two
33	  browsers a version apart rasterise text and shadows differently, so a comparison across them
34	  measures the renderer, not the product. Where the output is compared pixel by pixel, read the
35	  installed driver version at launch and **refuse to run** on any other, naming the pinned one in
36	  the error; where it is not — a build artifact, a behavioural assertion — let the build float
37	  and spend nothing on pinning it.
38	
39	- **Pinning is what buys a zero-diff browser golden — budget for the whole recipe or accept a
40	  tolerance.** A browser screenshot is not bit-stable across machines by default, which is why
41	  the general advice is a small tolerance. It *can* be made bit-stable, and the price is this
42	  pack's next two sections in full: the pinned build, a font jail, and the rasterisation flags.
43	  Take all of it or take the tolerance; a half-applied recipe gives a zero-diff gate that fails
44	  on someone else's machine for reasons no one can read off the diff.
45	
46	## The page's world is an input — replace all of it
47	
48	- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
49	  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
50	  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
51	  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
52	  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.
53	
54	- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
55	  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
56	  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
57	  has to be trusted.
58	
59	- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
60	  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
61	  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
62	  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
63	  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.
64	
65	- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
66	  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
67	  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
68	  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
69	  randomness and injected scripts are per page.
70	
71	- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
72	  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
73	  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
74	  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
75	  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
76	  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
77	  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
78	  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
79	  when they are fine.
80	
81	- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
82	  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
83	  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.
84	
85	- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
86	  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
87	  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
88	  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.
89	
90	- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
91	  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
92	  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
93	  has no timers to advance.
94	
95	## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts
96	
97	- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
98	  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
99	  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
100	  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
101	  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
102	  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
103	  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.
104	
105	- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
106	  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
107	  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
108	  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
109	  one machine.
110	
111	## Capturing
112	
113	- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
114	  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
115	  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
116	  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.
117	
118	- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
119	  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
120	  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
121	  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
122	  deliberately before measuring anything.
123	
124	- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
125	  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
126	  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
127	  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.
128	
129	- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
130	  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
131	  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
132	  is an error, not a crop.
133	
134	- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
135	  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
136	  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
137	  meant to show yourself.
138	
139	- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
140	  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
141	  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.
142

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# ArchUnit Overview

ArchUnit is described as: **"a free, simple and extensible library for checking the architecture of your Java code."**

## Key Example Components

The README demonstrates importing and testing with this pattern:

```java
JavaClasses importedClasses = new ClassFileImporter()
    .importPackages("com.myapp");

ArchRule rule = classes()...

rule.check(importedClasses);
```

The library enables developers to **"automatically test architecture and coding rules, using any plain Java unit testing framework"** by analyzing bytecode and constructing a queryable Java code structure.

The fluent API guides users through rule definition with methods like `classes().that().resideInAPackage()` to specify constraints on dependencies between packages, layers, and other structural concerns.

# Conftest: Policy Testing for Configuration Data

## What Conftest Does

"Conftest helps you write tests against structured configuration data." It works with Kubernetes manifests, Terraform, Tekton pipelines, and other configuration formats by leveraging the Rego language from Open Policy Agent.

## Rule Conventions

The tool evaluates policies using a specific naming convention. Rules prefixed with `deny`, `warn`, or `violation` are automatically assessed during testing. When violations are found, Conftest reports them with descriptive messages.

## The --combine Flag

When using the `--combine` flag, Conftest merges multiple input files into a single data structure. This enables policies to perform cross-file analysis and validation—useful when you need to verify relationships between separate configuration documents.

## Example Policy Structure

Here's a basic Rego pattern for denying non-compliant deployments:

```rego
deny contains msg if {
  input.kind == "Deployment"
  not input.spec.template.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg := "Containers must not run as root"
}
```

This demonstrates how Conftest policies examine configuration properties and generate failure messages when conditions aren't met.

If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. - pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Summary of runner.go

This file implements the core analysis execution engine for golangci-lint, which orchestrates how Go analyzers run across packages.

## Header Comment

The file begins with this explanation:

> "Package goanalysis defines the implementation of the checker commands. The same code drives the multi-analysis driver, the single-analysis driver that is conventionally provided for convenience along with each analysis package, and the test driver."

## Key Functionality

**Analyzer Orchestration**: The runner constructs a dependency graph of analysis actions, where each node represents one analyzer operating on one package. It handles both vertical dependencies (between packages) and horizontal dependencies (between analyzers).

**Fact Management**: The code registers and manages analysis facts across package boundaries. When an analyzer consumes or produces facts, it must run on a package's dependencies too, as indicated by this logic in `buildActionFactDeps`.

**Caching Integration**: The runner incorporates a package cache (`pkgCache`) and load guard to manage expensive operations, limiting parallel execution based on available CPU cores to balance memory and I/O usage.

**Parallel Execution**: The system loads and analyzes initial packages concurrently using goroutines, coordinated through a semaphore that restricts parallelism to `GOMAXPROCS`.

**Result Extraction**: After analysis completes, diagnostics are deduplicated by position and analyzer to prevent double-reporting in packages belonging to multiple test variants.

1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
     2	
     3	## 1. The layout is the contract
     4	
     5	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
     6	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
     7	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
     8	- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
     9	  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
    10	  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
    11	- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
    12	  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
    13	  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
    14	  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
    15	  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
    16	  not.
    17	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
    18	  kind field. Cases are
    19	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
    20	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
    21	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
    22	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
    23	- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
    24	  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
    25	  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
    26	  must be red.
    27	
    28	## 2. What the coverage gate checks
    29	
    30	The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
    31	(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
    32	registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
    33	image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
    34	stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
    35	edits the gate.
    36	
    37	The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
    38	owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
    39	precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
    40	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
    41	layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
    42	entry as `config.spec`.
    43	
    44	## 3. The kind vocabulary
    45	
    46	Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
    47	**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
    48	by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
    49	drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
    50	expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
    51	of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
    52	kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
    53	pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:
    54	
    55	- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
    56	  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
    57	  — the bijection stays strict.
    58	- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
    59	  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
    60	- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
    61	- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
    62	- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
    63	  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
    64	  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
    65	- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
    66	  never in the default loop.
    67	
    68	## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards
    69	
    70	Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
    71	time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
    72	arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
    73	states without losing the claim.
    74	
    75	- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
    76	  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
    77	- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
    78	- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
    79	  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
    80	- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
    81	  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.
    82	
    83	**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
    84	state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
    85	*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:
    86	
    87	- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
    88	  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
    89	  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
    90	- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
    91	  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
    92	  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
    93	  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
    94	  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
    95	- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
    96	  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.
    97	
    98	## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec
    99	
   100	A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:
   101	
   102	- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
   103	  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
   104	- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
   105	  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
   106	  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
   107	- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
   108	  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
   109	  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
   110	  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
   111	- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
   112	  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.
   113	
   114	## 6. Rendering recipes per stack
   115	
   116	- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
   117	  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
   118	  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
   119	  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
   120	- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
   121	  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
   122	  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
   123	  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
   124	  package and unit tests share it.
   125	- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
   126	  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
   127	  the threshold.
   128	
   129	## 7. The gallery is derived output
   130	
   131	- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
   132	  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
   133	  captioned storyboard strip.
   134	- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
   135	  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.
   136	
   137	## 8. Refresh is a review step
   138	
   139	One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
   140	cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
   141	for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
   142	procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
   143	writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.

1	# spec-driven-product — shipping against an executable spec
     2	
     3	## 1. The executable spec is the backbone
     4	
     5	- **One numbered requirements document states what the product must do**, leaf by leaf: what each
     6	  surface must render, how it must behave, the exact copy and semantics it must carry. Not prose
     7	  aspirations — specific, testable statements.
     8	- **Keep the spec's boundary crisp: a leaf is what the harness can assert.** The feature-level story —
     9	  what the product does and why — lives in the product's prose docs; the spec holds the specific,
    10	  testable statements (exact strings, placement, semantics). A statement no kind can prove isn't a
    11	  leaf yet: it stays prose, or it's the trigger to add the kind that can prove it.
    12	- **Every leaf carries a stable id.** Add new requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse
    13	  a retired one — the ids are what cases, commits, and review discussion key on. (1)
    14	- **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf with no executable proof fails the build until a case
    15	  claims it. (2)
    16	- **The spec drives the tests, never the other way around.** A behavior change starts by editing the
    17	  leaf, watching the gate go red, then changing product and proof to match. A test changed without its
    18	  leaf — or a leaf reworded to match what the code happens to do — inverts the authority.
    19	
    20	## 2. Every leaf ⇄ exactly one proof, of the right kind
    21	
    22	- **Enforce the bijection with a committed coverage gate**: each leaf claimed by exactly one case,
    23	  each case claiming exactly one leaf, and every discovered kind of case actually executed by a
    24	  runner. The gate is part of the project's own suite.
    25	- **A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted** — a rendered-state snapshot, a driven gesture,
    26	  a pure rule, a boundary-enforced rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually observe what it
    27	  asserts. Keep kinds **extensible** — adding one is a self-contained drop. (3)
    28	- **A kind may be a singleton.** "The product loads in the real environment" is a perfectly good leaf
    29	  whose mechanism is one end-to-end case; the kind names the *way of asserting*, not a population of
    30	  cases.
    31	- **Give each kind's runner a named lane, and keep the default lane fast and deterministic.** Heavy
    32	  real-environment kinds gate the merge from CI without slowing the inner loop; their trust rules
    33	  (twice-green before merging, self-diagnosing on failure) are canon in the writing-tests skill.
    34	- **Actuals come from the real code.** Whatever the kind, the proof drives the shipped entry points
    35	  under a faithful harness — never a parallel re-implementation of what production "should" do (the
    36	  writing-tests skill owns the general rule).
    37	
    38	## 3. Expected results are owner-owned
    39	
    40	- **The committed expecteds are the owner's approval record of the product.** A case's success
    41	  criterion encodes what the owner accepted. (4)
    42	- **The contract takes two honest shapes.** *Artifact-expected* (a committed render, an exact-values
    43	  file): the owner approves a committed file — an agent may **propose** the expected for a brand-new
    44	  leaf, but never modifies a committed one to make a failing case pass. *Coded-expected* (an
    45	  assertion, a `verify()`): the expected **is** the assertion — keep it outside the write surface of
    46	  whatever writes the product code, so passing by weakening the check isn't even expressible.
    47	- **On a mismatch, surface actual vs. expected (and the diff) and ask.** The re-baselining procedure —
    48	  diff shown, owner approves, only then re-baseline — is canon in the writing-tests skill, and it
    49	  applies uniformly: to a moved render, a changed values file, and a failing assertion alike. (5)
    50	- **Expected changes ride the normal review flow** — they land in the diff like code, so the owner
    51	  approves the product change and its new expected together, once.
    52	
    53	## 4. State a requirement once; prove it at every boundary that enforces it
    54	
    55	- **A product rule with more than one enforcing tier gets sibling leaves under one statement** — e.g.
    56	  "only signed-in users can post": the surface's half (the client sends credentials) and the
    57	  boundary's half (the server rejects an unauthenticated write) are separate proofs of one
    58	  requirement.
    59	- **The proof lives where the rule is actually enforced.** A surface-side test of a server-enforced
    60	  rule proves only that the client cooperates, not that the boundary holds; if the real enforcement is
    61	  the backend, a leaf must exist there, exercised against the real handler.
    62	
    63	## 5. A supported-targets matrix is spec, not folklore
    64	
    65	- **When part of the product's value is breadth over external targets** — supported sites, file
    66	  formats, providers, locales — each supported target is its own leaf, so dropping a target is a
    67	  visible spec change, not a silent regression.
    68	- **Prove each target against a committed, real sample of it** (a captured page, a genuine file), with
    69	  the owner-reviewed exact-values expectation committed beside it — capture the sample first and read
    70	  the expecteds off the committed bytes (canon in the writing-tests skill). A hand-invented sample
    71	  proves support for a target the world doesn't actually serve.
    72	- **Adding a target is a documented, repeatable flow** that lands the new leaf, its real sample, and
    73	  its reviewed expected together.
    74	
    75	## 6. Green means "claimed", not "fully verified" — track the gap honestly
    76	
    77	- **Say what the harness cannot reach, naming the exact boundary of each stub.** A faithful harness is
    78	  still a model of the platform; the honest sentence pattern is "this proof confirms our code *asks*
    79	  for the action, not that the platform *performs* it". Put that statement where readers of the spec
    80	  will see it — a banner on the requirements doc, linking the issue that tracks closing the gap —
    81	  rather than in a test README footnote.
    82	- **Deliberate gaps are marked at the leaf and committed, never remembered.** A leaf that can't be
    83	  faithfully verified yet stays in the spec, visibly provisional (a loud "to be decided" marker, and a
    84	  pointer to whatever covers it meanwhile), and is listed in a committed allowlist the coverage gate
    85	  checks — the allowlist is the burn-down list, shrunk deliberately. Prefer a real validation; reach
    86	  for the marker only for a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired harness.
    87	
    88	## 7. The owner reviews the product surface, not the internals
    89	
    90	- **Embed regenerated renders of the real states in the spec itself** — the requirements document
    91	  doubles as a gallery of what the product actually shows, generated from the shipped code, so
    92	  approving the spec *is* approving the product's appearance.
    93	- **Regenerate, never hand-edit.** The gallery is derived output of a committed generator; fixing it
    94	  means fixing the source (or the generator) and regenerating. (6)
    95	- **The deterministic golden-image method this leans on is canon in the writing-tests skill** —
    96	  matching the render engine to the surface (a bit-exact rasterizer for inline-styled/SVG surfaces, a
    97	  headless browser for pages that use grid/vars/emoji/form-widgets), bundled fonts, capturing a
    98	  host-page surface with styles inlined, and a drift gate on the embedded gallery.
    99	
   100	## 8. Ship automatically while `main` stays green
   101	
   102	- **`main` is releasable at all times, and automation does the releasing** — a release (and, where
   103	  the platform has one, store publication) cuts from `main` on its own cadence without a human build
   104	  step. Keeping `main` green *is* the release gate: a red `main` is a shipping outage, fixed before
   105	  new work.
   106	- **The version users see moves deliberately.** Automation may patch-bump to ship, but a meaningful
   107	  version change is a decision made on `main`, not a side effect. The concrete release contract —
   108	  workflows, artifacts, store procedures — belongs to the project's release pack or release doc, not
   109	  here.

1	# Chrome extensions
     2	
     3	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building
     4	> or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the
     5	> [chrome-store-releases standard](skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md) and copy its canonical
     6	> workflows instead of re-deriving them.
     7	
     8	## Service worker
     9	
    10	- **Handing a path to a Chrome API or `fetch` from an MV3 service worker** (`importScripts`,
    11	  `action.setIcon`) — make it extension-root absolute: a leading slash, or
    12	  `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file
    13	  location, not the extension root, and a bare relative path fails silently — it can abort the
    14	  worker on import, or make an API call reject while the worker keeps running.
    15	
    16	- **Wanting `import`/`export` in extension code** — MV3 loads ES modules natively; don't add a
    17	  bundler just to use them. Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel
    18	  scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension.
    19	  Content scripts are the exception — they are classic scripts, below.
    20	
    21	## Content scripts
    22	
    23	- **Assembling a shared global from several injected content-script files** — **augment** it,
    24	  never replace it: merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`. The files are
    25	  re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), so replacing makes each
    26	  newly-injected file wipe what earlier files already attached.
    27	
    28	- **Accumulating state in a file that is re-injected** (e.g. a list a source pushes into) — reset
    29	  it at load time.
    30	
    31	- **Loading ES module code into a content script** — register a tiny **classic loader** whose only
    32	  statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`. A **registered or static content
    33	  script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module**:
    34	  `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as
    35	  classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or
    36	  the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws
    37	  `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's
    38	  console, not the extension's**. Dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it
    39	  pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface
    40	  intact.
    41	
    42	- **Adding an import to a content-script module** — list that module **and its whole transitive
    43	  import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins), or the fetch is
    44	  blocked.
    45	
    46	- **Keeping that `web_accessible_resources` list correct** — have a test walk the import graph
    47	  from the entry module, so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
    48	
    49	## Permissions and host access
    50	
    51	- **Matching a host with `chrome.events.UrlFilter`** — its host operators are **raw string
    52	  matches, not domain-boundary matches**: `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches
    53	  `evilexample.com`, and `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or
    54	  page condition on exactly these filters. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine
    55	  `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label
    56	  boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
    57	
    58	- **Running a content script on arbitrary third-party pages without an install-time host warning**
    59	  — request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the
    60	  (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real
    61	  foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then
    62	  register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a
    63	  static `content_scripts` entry.
    64	
    65	- **Starting the service worker when a runtime-granted permission is in play** — reconcile your
    66	  stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to
    67	  match, on every start. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you.
    68	
    69	- **A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser** — `host_permissions` does not bypass CORS.
    70	  Listing a host lets the extension's fetches *reach* it, but the server must still return CORS
    71	  headers for the extension origin (`chrome-extension://<id>`) or the request fails.
    72	
    73	- **Reaching your *own* backend** — don't add a `host_permissions` entry merely for that: if it
    74	  already returns permissive CORS the fetch succeeds without one, and the entry only adds a scary
    75	  install-time host-access warning.
    76	
    77	## Sign-in and tokens
    78	
    79	- **Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend** (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any
    80	  OIDC-validating server) — obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow`
    81	  (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**,
    82	  redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`),
    83	  scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Pin the extension id with a
    84	  manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` —
    85	  it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT
    86	  authorizer rejects.
    87	
    88	- **Refreshing a token silently** (`launchWebAuthFlow({interactive:false})`) — request
    89	  `prompt=none`. `prompt=consent` always needs interaction and therefore always fails silently —
    90	  reserve it (or omit `prompt`) for the interactive fallback.
    91	
    92	- **Refreshing silently with more than one account signed in** — pass the remembered account's
    93	  email as `login_hint`; otherwise the provider can't tell which session to reuse and forces an
    94	  interactive account-picker. Persist the non-secret email from the first successful sign-in.
    95	
    96	- **Storing a token** — extension storage is unencrypted, so treat tokens as secrets at rest: keep
    97	  the bearer/ID token in in-memory `chrome.storage.session` (cleared on browser exit) and persist
    98	  only non-secret identifiers (e.g. the account email) to `chrome.storage.local`.
    99	
   100	- **Wanting a token to survive a browser restart** — re-run the silent flow; don't switch to a
   101	  refresh-token flow just for that, which puts a longer-lived credential on disk.
   102	
   103	## Extension UI surfaces
   104	
   105	- **Knowing whether your side panel is open** — have the panel open a `Port` on load and read its
   106	  connect/disconnect as open/closed. MV3 gives the side panel no is-open/close API, and an action
   107	  popup suppresses `action.onClicked`.
   108	
   109	- **Opening the side panel programmatically** — `chrome.sidePanel.open()` needs Chrome 116+, so
   110	  raise `minimum_chrome_version` accordingly.
   111	
   112	- **Putting a menu on the toolbar icon itself** — create it with
   113	  `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })`; the `contextMenus` permission carries
   114	  **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission).
   115	
   116	- **Recreating those menu items on install or startup** — call `contextMenus.removeAll()` first,
   117	  so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top
   118	  level.
   119	
   120	## Introspecting a service worker over CDP
   121	
   122	- **Awaiting a `chrome.*` callback API inside `Runtime.evaluate`** — don't: they don't reliably
   123	  settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout). Build the awaited
   124	  signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead.
   125	
   126	- **Reading a worker value from an injected evaluate** — a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't
   127	  reachable from one, so expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`.
   128	
   129	- **Attaching to a dormant worker** — poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately
   130	  after attaching. A dormant worker has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to
   131	  it is what starts that.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about cross-file linting and multi-file rules in ESLint:

## Key Findings

ESLint today does not have any native concepts of cross-file dependencies, stateful parsing, or type information. This is a significant limitation for implementing multi-file linting rules.

### RFC Discussions

The suggestions from typescript-eslint were not accepted in the ESLint RFC process regarding cross-file linting support. Several RFCs have been proposed over the years:

- eslint/eslint#14139 (early 2021): a proposal for an API to allow plugins to up-front initialization/setup work, with extensive notes about how type-aware linting worked and what should be implemented.
- eslint/rfcs#102 feat: parsing session objects (late 2022 through early 2023): a request for information needed to optimize cross-file linting.

### Multithread Linting RFC

There are concerns that if multithread linting is implemented without consideration for multifile analysis, the cost of implementing multi-file analysis later would skyrocket and likely prevent it from ever being implemented.

### Current Status

TypeScript-eslint hopes that ESLint will evolve long-term to support cross-file, stateful linting as needed for typed linting. However, this remains an open challenge for the project.

content.content:
1	# macOS
     2	
     3	## The app bundle is assembled, not built
     4	
     5	- **SwiftPM builds a binary; nothing builds you a `.app`.** `swift build -c release` yields an
     6	  executable — the bundle (`Contents/MacOS/<exe>`, `Contents/Info.plist`,
     7	  `Contents/Resources/`) is assembled by your own script. Keep that script the single place the
     8	  bundle's shape is defined, so the local build and CI produce byte-identical layouts.
     9	- **Commit one high-resolution icon master and generate the `.icns`** in the build script (`sips`
    10	  to each size into an `.iconset`, then `iconutil -c icns`). Both tools ship with macOS, so the
    11	  repo carries one PNG instead of ten, and the icon can't half-update.
    12	- **A menu-bar-only app is `LSUIElement: true`** in `Info.plist` — that, not code, is what removes
    13	  the Dock icon and the main window.
    14	- **Pin `LSMinimumSystemVersion` to the same OS version the package's `platforms:` declares.** They
    15	  are two independent claims about the same floor, and only one of them is enforced at launch.
    16	
    17	## TCC and the Hardened Runtime are two different gates — know which applies
    18	
    19	- **Reaching for a protected resource** — give it its own **usage-description string** in
    20	  `Info.plist`, the text the user consents to; without one the app is killed rather than prompted.
    21	  Capabilities that feel like one feature take separate keys — an app that listens *and*
    22	  transcribes needs `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription`, or
    23	  is killed at whichever it forgot — and only *some* resources also need a codesign entitlement,
    24	  and only under the Hardened Runtime.
    25	
    26	- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`), and under it a
    27	  resource-access exception must be granted explicitly by entitlement — device capture
    28	  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, camera) is the classic one. So **turning on
    29	  notarization can silently break a capability an ad-hoc build had**, because the ad-hoc build was
    30	  never running under the restriction. Ship the entitlement in the same change as the runtime flag.
    31	- **Capabilities gated purely by TCC plus their usage string need no entitlement at all** (speech
    32	  recognition is the worked example). Adding one you don't need is noise; omitting one you do need
    33	  is a runtime failure no build step catches.
    34	- **Do not enable the App Sandbox on the Developer ID track.** The sandbox belongs to the Mac App
    35	  Store lane, needs a different (Apple Distribution) certificate, and silently removes
    36	  capabilities the direct-download build has — distributed notifications, for one.
    37	
    38	## Speech recognition leaves the machine unless you say it must not
    39	
    40	- **`SFSpeechRecognizer` streams audio to Apple's servers by default.** On-device recognition is
    41	  opt-in, and the opt-in is a property of the **request**
    42	  (`request.requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true`), not of the recognizer — so it has to be set on
    43	  every request the app builds, and a new call site added later starts out server-side. Nothing in
    44	  the build says which mode ran; the difference is only visible in what left the machine.
    45	- **The opt-in is only honourable where the locale's model is installed.** `supportsOnDeviceRecognition`
    46	  is per-recognizer and false until then, and requiring on-device recognition where it isn't
    47	  supported fails the request rather than quietly falling back — so check it and decide the degrade
    48	  deliberately (refuse the feature, or say plainly that this locale would transcribe off-device).
    49	- Speech is TCC-gated, so it needs its usage string and **no** entitlement — see the section above.
    50	
    51	## Keep signing and notarization an optional, secret-gated lane
    52	
    53	- **The unsigned path must stay a working path.** Gate the Developer ID + notarization steps on the
    54	  signing secrets being present, and ship an **ad-hoc-signed** artifact when they aren't. Make
    55	  signing a required step and every fork, and every build in a repo whose secrets aren't set, goes
    56	  red for a reason unrelated to the change.
    57	- **An ad-hoc signature cannot be notarized.** They are separate lanes, not degrees of the same
    58	  one: only an identity-signed bundle can be submitted to the notary service. Don't write a
    59	  pipeline that "tries" to notarize whatever it just signed.
    60	- **Notarize the distributed container, then staple it** (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler
    61	  staple` and `stapler validate`). Stapling is what makes the download open offline without a
    62	  round-trip to Apple; skipping it works on your machine and fails on a user's.
    63	- **In CI, an imported identity must be in the searchable keychain list.** Creating an ephemeral
    64	  keychain, importing the `.p12` and setting the key partition list is not enough —
    65	  `codesign` searches the *user's keychain list*, so the new keychain has to be added to it or the
    66	  identity is simply not found.
    67	- **Say out loud, in a build annotation, which lane ran.** "No signing secret — publishing an
    68	  ad-hoc build" turns a silently-degraded artifact into a visible one.
    69	
    70	## Distribution and the Gatekeeper story you owe the user
    71	
    72	- **A drag-to-install DMG is a staged folder, not Finder scripting.** Stage the `.app` beside a
    73	  symlink to `/Applications`, drop the icon in as `.VolumeIcon.icns`, flag the folder as having a
    74	  custom icon, and let `hdiutil create` carry it through. Anything that automates Finder to lay out
    75	  the window is fragile in CI and unnecessary.
    76	- **Write the Gatekeeper bypass for the OS your users are on.** macOS 15 removed the
    77	  right-click → *Open* bypass; the current path is System Settings → Privacy & Security →
    78	  *Open Anyway*, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>`. An install doc that still says
    79	  right-click → Open reads as broken software.
    80	- **A notarized build should need none of that** — if your README's manual-bypass section is the
    81	  one users actually follow, the signing lane isn't running.
    82	
    83	## Assume the user's Mac has no developer toolchain
    84	
    85	- **Diagnostics belong inside the shipped app**, or in a script using only what ships with macOS.
    86	  Anything requiring a compiler on the user's machine is a diagnostic that will never be run.
    87	- **`command -v swift` does not test for a Swift toolchain.** `/usr/bin/swift` exists on every Mac
    88	  as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer tools?"* dialog when invoked — so
    89	  the probe passes and the script asks the user to install several gigabytes of Xcode. Gate on
    90	  `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1`, which fails quietly when the tools are absent.
    91	
    92	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit"
    93	
    94	- **`NSApplication` installs no signal handlers.** `NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the
    95	  logout/shutdown Apple Event) runs `applicationWillTerminate`; a bare `SIGTERM` (Activity
    96	  Monitor's Quit, `killall`), `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` kills the process with **no** teardown. Route
    97	  them through a `DispatchSourceSignal` into `NSApp.terminate` — and set `signal(sig, SIG_IGN)`
    98	  **before** `resume()`, or a signal arriving in the gap still takes the fatal default.
    99	  `SIGKILL`, Force Quit and a crash stay uncoverable; name that as residual risk rather than
   100	  claiming coverage.
   101	- **An uncaught Objective-C exception is an exit path too.** It aborts the process, so no teardown
   102	  runs; a framework call that *raises* (rather than throws) is therefore a resource-release bug as
   103	  well as a crash. Swift cannot catch `NSException` — a tiny Objective-C target of your own is the
   104	  only trap, and it is only safe around calls that validate before mutating.
   105	
   106	## Sleep, wake, and deferred work
   107	
   108	- **There is no "the machine is back" notification.** `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` also fires
   109	  for a dark/Power-Nap wake with nobody there. Fan in the several signals that a real return emits
   110	  (wake, screens wake, session became active, the screen-unlocked distributed notification) and
   111	  **coalesce them** — a genuine return fires a burst, and each must not schedule its own work.
   112	- **Coalesce with an id, not a boolean.** A single `pending` flag deadlocks: something invalidates
   113	  the timer, the timer clears the flag, and whichever ordering loses leaves the next wake either
   114	  unable to schedule or double-scheduling. Hold the in-flight work's id; a stale timer compares its
   115	  captured id and returns.
   116	- **`asyncAfter` work scheduled before sleep fires immediately on wake.** Give every intentional
   117	  stop a generation counter, capture the generation when scheduling, and abort in the closure if it
   118	  moved — otherwise deferred work reacquires resources on the way *into* sleep or before the
   119	  machine has settled. When cancelling in-flight work, reset the latches beside it too, or they
   120	  stay stuck and block everything after.
   121	- **Measure a span that includes a sleep with `Date()`, not `ProcessInfo.systemUptime`.** The
   122	  monotonic clock does not advance while the machine sleeps — which is exactly the span you are
   123	  trying to measure. Use `systemUptime` for the opposite question ("how long, while we were
   124	  awake").
   125	
   126	## Holding a device the user can unplug
   127	
   128	- **Release the device on every path where capture ends.** A process that dies with its IO proc
   129	  still registered can leave some USB devices wedged until physically re-plugged. This is necessary
   130	  and *not sufficient* — a device can also wedge below the user-space audio daemon, where no
   131	  teardown of yours helps.
   132	- **Never construct a capture engine to ask whether a device exists.** Materializing an input node
   133	  opens the default device and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device; a retry ladder built on
   134	  that is not a cheap probe but an open/close plus an aggregate create-and-destroy, repeated for as
   135	  long as the hardware is missing. Query the HAL's device properties instead — a property read
   136	  opens nothing and can be sampled forever for free. The churn is observable rather than
   137	  theoretical: each hidden aggregate appears in the HAL as `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`, so
   138	  what a retry ladder is really doing can be counted instead of argued about.
   139	- **Presence is not usability, at either layer.** Mid-teardown a device enumerates as alive with an
   140	  unreadable name and a **zero** sample rate. Require a nonzero rate and a sane channel count, and
   141	  judge the *system default* input — a healthy device behind a broken default is not one you can
   142	  capture from. One layer up, the engine lies in the opposite direction: with the input torn down,
   143	  the input node's `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports a plausible 48 kHz while its
   144	  `inputFormat` reports 0, so a guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that
   145	  cannot succeed — read both and require them to agree. Whatever a new probe reads, ask what that
   146	  field says while the device is absent.
   147	- **A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N seconds" is only
   148	  as good as the observation behind it: a state maintained by a timer must be **seeded at start**
   149	  (a repeating timer does not fire immediately) and **invalidated across any gap** — a sleep is a
   150	  gap, and carrying a settle clock straight through one makes the gate inert on exactly the
   151	  transition it was built for. Model "not observed" as its own state, distinct from "absent", and
   152	  key the span on the device's **UID** — an unplug-and-replug, or a swap for a different mic, is a
   153	  new arrival that starts its own clock rather than inheriting the departed device's.
   154	- **"Started" is not "working".** A running engine delivering buffers of pure silence looks
   155	  identical to a healthy one from the inside. Measure what actually arrives, publish a health state
   156	  the UI renders, and when a failure mode has exactly one remedy, name **that** remedy rather than
   157	  the generic one.
   158	- **Compile-green is not a gate for device code.** `swift build` cannot see a raise-vs-throw bug or
   159	  a lifecycle race, and both are reachable in the first second of a run. A change here is not
   160	  verified until the app has actually launched on a Mac. Reaching the interesting case needs no
   161	  hardware theatre: let the display sleep and `coreaudiod` tears its device contexts down seconds
   162	  later, which is the same transition as an unplug from the app's point of view.
