1	# Flutter
     2	
     3	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
     4	
     5	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
     6	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
     7	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
     8	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
     9	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
    10	  the plugin's platform channels.
    11	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
    12	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak.
    13	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
    14	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
    15	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
    16	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
    17	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
    18	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
    19	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
    20	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
    21	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
    22	
    23	## Widget tests and goldens
    24	
    25	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
    26	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
    27	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
    28	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
    29	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
    30	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
    31	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
    32	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
    33	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
    34	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
    35	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
    36	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
    37	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
    38	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
    39	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
    40	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
    41	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
    42	  the harness default.
    43	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
    44	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
    45	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
    46	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
    47	
    48	## Toolchain habits
    49	
    50	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
    51	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
    52	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
    53	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
    54	- **`pubspec.lock` moving without `pubspec.yaml` moving is version skew, not a dependency change.**
    55	  An app commits its lockfile (only a *library* package gitignores it), so the file is tracked on
    56	  purpose — the thing to keep out of the diff is the churn a local `flutter pub get` produces when
    57	  the installed SDK resolves differently from CI's. Unless you deliberately ran an upgrade, revert
    58	  it: `git checkout -- pubspec.lock`.
    59	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
    60	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
    61	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
    62	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
    63	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
    64	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
    65	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
    66	- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
    67	  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
    68	  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
    69	  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
    70	  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
    71	  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
    72	  Part 9).

# web-scraping pack

Declared (opt-in) by a project whose input is **another organisation's website**,
reached without a contract: no support channel, no changelog, no SLA. No
fingerprint — a scraper is ordinary HTTP client code, indistinguishable from a call
to an API the project owns.

Prose plus one skill, and no checks: every rule is about a *remote* service's
behaviour (which field is authoritative, whether an instant is UTC, when a 200 is a
bot wall), none of which is written into repo state in a shape a check could read
without firing on ordinary HTTP code.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adding a source, or what to parse | medium | complexity | prose: 90 words |
| A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record | medium | correctness | prose: 31 words |
| Learning something non-obvious by probing the service | medium | complexity | prose: 71 words |
| Writing the fetch itself | medium | correctness | prose: 44 words |
| Deciding whether to retry a failed request | medium | correctness | prose: 43 words |
| Porting a fetch to an HTTP client | medium | correctness | prose: 47 words |
| Setting the retry budget | medium | performance | prose: 38 words |
| One item in a batch failing | high | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| A sandbox refusing the target host | critical | legal | prose: 80 words |
| A fetch that fails only in CI | medium | correctness | prose: 108 words |
| Needing many items with no list endpoint | medium | performance | prose: 66 words |
| A fetch that cannot produce a page | medium | correctness | prose: 66 words |
| Deciding whether a fetch succeeded | high | correctness | prose: 55 words |
| Getting an empty body back | high | correctness | prose: 36 words |
| Choosing which field to read | high | correctness | prose: 57 words |
| Filtering rows by a status | high | correctness | prose: 40 words |
| Reading a numeric field | high | correctness | prose: 17 words |
| Reducing a set to its cheapest | medium | correctness | prose: 45 words |
| Converting an instant to local time | high | correctness | prose: 132 words |
| Taking a "now" | high | correctness | prose: 38 words |
| Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous | high | correctness | prose: 129 words |
| Changing the conversion | high | correctness | prose: 78 words |
| Emitting a value the pipeline hasn't reached | high | correctness | prose: 64 words |
| Deciding what a fetch writes to disk | medium | complexity | prose: 128 words |
| Re-running a fetch that already ran | medium | correctness | prose: 70 words |
| Scheduling the refresh | medium | correctness | prose: 75 words |
| Generating artifacts from the stored data | medium | correctness | prose: 55 words |

## Skill

| Skill | Trigger |
|---|---|
| [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) | adding a new source, or an existing one stopped parsing — locate the surface and write the reference doc before any parser exists |

Provenance: distilled from three fleet members that each take data from a site they
don't own.

| Member | What it evidenced |
|---|---|
| `missingbulb/EdFringeNow` | `scraper/SCRAPING.md` + `scraper/README.md` + `fetch_shows.py` / `fetch_prices.py` / `normalize.py`: the empty-SPA-shell → client GraphQL API read, reading the site's own JS bundles for the operation surface, the reference-doc-so-nothing-re-probes discipline, resumable paging with randomized delays, the status-enum-over-boolean and amounts-as-strings traps, UTC-at-the-edge, unknown≠free, alias batching with halve-on-reject, per-field refresh cadence, and derived-outputs-as-a-pure-function-of-the-master |
| `missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` | `edfringe/fetch.py` + `edfringe/extract.py`: the hydration-blob surface, the git-ignored HTML cache vs the committed raw record with offline re-derivation, fetch-only-what's-missing, browser-like headers with exponential backoff, bot-challenge detection, deny-listing bad statuses, record-and-continue reporting, and its own UTC→local edge conversion |
| `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator` | its extractor-pipeline rules and `scraperapi.mjs`: one fetching module as the whole surface, the rendering proxy with a wait-for-selector, the retryable-status set and how a rewrite drops it, empty-body-means-nothing-rendered, non-deterministic rendered output, preferring JSON-LD/`og:` over DOM positions, sandbox bot-blocking with the credential held by a runner, and unfetchable-page-is-a-dead-end |

Every rule above appears in at least two of the three, except the alias-batching and
per-field-cadence rules (**Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint**,
**Scheduling the refresh**), which are one member's — kept because they are plainly
general to any rate-limited source and their evidence is concrete.

## Consolidated into this pack

Once the facet had a home, prose that had been mis-homed for want of one moved here.
Each was already written; none is new material.

| What moved | From | Landed in |
|---|---|---|
| The datacenter-IP diagnosis: a fetch that works locally and 403s from CI is the IP, not the User-Agent; the residential/rendering proxy is the answer, and a target still blocked through it is un-cacheable | the baseline prose (deleted there in this change) | **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** |
| Cross a time zone exactly once, at the ingest edge — including the downstream double-conversion and the device-clock "now" | `missingbulb/EdFringeNow`'s local `edfringe-data` pack | **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** (landed with the pack) and **Taking a "now"** |
| A conversion change is a full-snapshot change: regenerate from the raw record, and expect the boundary to move records between partitions | `missingbulb/EdFringeNow`'s local `edfringe-data` pack | **Changing the conversion** |
| Read an ambiguous value by what the page declares, centrally — the numeric slash date resolved from a positive locale signal, and `Z` as serialization rather than the subject's zone | `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`'s local `gcec` pack | **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** |

The basics deletion is done here. The two members' local copies are theirs to prune —
this session has no write access to either — so they are left for `growth-dedup` to
drop once this pack is declared there.

# headless-browser pack

Active when the repo references a browser-automation driver in JS/TS source — a `playwright` /
`playwright-core` / `puppeteer` / `puppeteer-core` module specifier, or a `.launch(` call site.
Scanning source rather than a dependency manifest is deliberate: a repo can drive a browser its
environment image already installs, with no dependency entry anywhere to find.

Prose only. Every rule is a runtime browser behaviour or a judgment about a harness's shape,
neither of which has a repo-state signature a check could read without asserting that a
particular call still exists — the shape the corpus rejects outright.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolve binary, never download | high | correctness | prose: 123 words |
| Reinstalling the driver repeats the download danger | high | correctness | prose: 130 words |
| Stub an unvendored CDN library's API | medium | correctness | prose: 114 words |
| Pin the build for pixels | high | correctness | prose: 87 words |
| Zero-diff costs whole recipe | medium | correctness | prose: 95 words |
| Fake origin, abort by default | high | correctness | prose: 80 words |
| `https` origin for geolocation | medium | correctness | prose: 48 words |
| Route vendored assets host-agnostically | medium | correctness | prose: 75 words |
| Context knobs vs page knobs | medium | correctness | prose: 67 words |
| Window-size flag isn't a viewport | high | correctness | prose: 132 words |
| Fakes as init scripts | high | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| CSS freeze misses `element.animate` | high | correctness | prose: 45 words |
| Two clock modes | medium | correctness | prose: 55 words |
| Font jail, not just webfonts | high | correctness | prose: 111 words |
| Reproducible rasterisation flags | high | correctness | prose: 60 words |
| Wait on the page's signal | high | correctness | prose: 66 words |
| Clip, don't screenshot the element | medium | correctness | prose: 65 words |
| Bounding boxes go stale | medium | correctness | prose: 59 words |
| Whole-pixel clips | medium | correctness | prose: 57 words |
| Strip scripts needing the runtime | medium | correctness | prose: 53 words |
| One browser, many contexts | medium | performance | prose: 51 words |

## Boundary

This pack is the browser itself. Which engine a UI golden should use, the tolerance it may carry,
self-skipping where no browser is present, the re-baselining approval gate, and wiring the run into
a workflow are all deliberately not here — the "zero-diff costs the whole recipe" rule is written to
complement that testing guidance rather than restate or contradict it.

Provenance: distilled from three fleet members that drive a browser from code, independently and
for different reasons. `missingbulb/EdFringeNow` — a pinned-Chromium visual-requirements harness:
fake-origin routing, the font jail, rasterisation flags, clip and bounding-box mechanics.
`missingbulb/CrosswordChat` — browser rasterisation for both goldens and generated build
artifacts: environment binary resolution, stripping runtime-dependent scripts.
`missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` — an interactive responsive check: the window-size-is-not-a-
viewport footgun and the virtual-time budget. The first two solved the cross-machine rendering
problem two different ways, which is what the pinning rules carry.
`missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` holds a vestigial fourth instance in a retired prototype.

---
name: map-a-data-source
description: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
---

# Map a data source before you parse it

This runs **once per source** (and again when a site is redesigned). Its output is
not code — it is a committed reference doc plus one saved raw payload. Everything
after it is ordinary parsing.

## 1. Fetch one page and look at what came back

Save the raw response of a single representative page to disk and read it. You are
answering one question: **is the data in this document?**

- If the interesting rows are present in the markup, you have a server-rendered page
  — go to step 2.
- If you got a small shell (a few KB of script tags and an empty root), the page is a
  single-page app and the data arrives separately — go to step 3.

## 2. Look for a hydration blob first

A server-rendered app framework almost always embeds the exact object it rendered
from in a script tag with a stable id. Search the saved document for a large inline
JSON payload and find the path to the record you want (it is usually nested a few
levels under a props/data wrapper).

If one exists, **this is the surface**: it is the site's own typed record, one regex
and one JSON parse away, and it does not care about the layout. Save that object,
verbatim, as your first committed fixture.

If there is no blob, the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD `<script
type="application/ld+json">`, `og:` meta tags) is the next-best target — it survives
redesigns that break element selectors.

## 3. Find the client API

Identify the request the page makes for its rows. Two ways in, and the second one
matters more than it sounds:

- **Watch the page load** in browser devtools and read the request: URL, method,
  headers, auth, and the response shape.
- **Read the site's own JavaScript bundles.** Fetch the page, extract the script
  `src` paths (mind any asset prefix — the paths in the HTML already carry it),
  download them, and search for the operation names, query documents and field
  selections. For a GraphQL client the embedded query strings unescape into readable
  SDL, giving you the **complete** set of operations and fields the client was built
  against — the authoritative surface, short of introspection.

  This path is worth knowing because it needs **only the public site host**. When the
  API host is blocked from where you are but the site itself loads, reading its
  bundle still tells you exactly what a request would look like. It cannot execute
  anything, so it is not a bypass of the block.

Then note the auth story. A public listing is frequently reachable with anonymous
credentials the client itself ships — the same read access every visitor has. If
reaching the data requires a real account, stop and take that to the owner.

## 4. Probe the shape, not just the happy path

Before declaring the surface mapped, ask these of it explicitly, because each one has
silently corrupted a pipeline that assumed otherwise:

- **Are timestamps UTC or local?** Take one item whose real-world time you can verify
  independently and check.
- **Which field is authoritative for state?** If there is both a status enum and a
  summarizing boolean, find an item where they disagree — there usually is one.
- **What are the enum's legal values?** Take them from the service's own options
  endpoint, not from the sample you happened to pull.
- **Are numbers numbers?** Amounts and counts frequently arrive as strings.
- **Is anything missing from this surface entirely?** A listing endpoint often
  carries flags but no amounts, with the real values behind a separate per-item
  query. Find that out now, not after you've shipped a catalogue of nulls.
- **Is there a bulk form?** If the per-item query has no list variant, check whether
  one *request* can still carry many items (GraphQL aliases, a multi-id parameter).

## 5. Write it down, then stop

Commit a reference doc beside the scripts holding: the endpoint(s) and auth, the
field surface, the enum values, each answer from step 4, and — explicitly — the
questions you could **not** answer and where they'd have to come from. State the
access constraint too: which hosts are reachable from where, and which sanctioned job
is allowed to do the fetching.

The bar: **a later session should be able to write the parser from this doc without
touching the live service.** If it can't, the reconnaissance isn't finished.

- **D** action-time: the signature is in a TOOL CALL's input before it runs — a Bash command shape, an MCP GitHub tool's arguments (a PR body, an issue body, missing `fields`/`per_page`), a file path a tool targets, a WebFetch URL. State tool + pattern. (These become a declared PreToolUse guard that blocks or warns, with a Stop-time transcript scan as backstop.)
- **E** conversation/transcript: the signature is in the session transcript — a reply's shape, a tool-call sequence or count, a skill loaded or not, a wait/poll pattern. State it.
- **F** procedure/judgment with a NAMEABLE deterministic trigger: not checkable, but the moment it applies is detectable — a specific tool call (e.g. `mcp__github__create_pull_request`, a Bash `git commit`), a prompt phrase, a file path pattern, a session event, a task/worker kind. It belongs in a skill loaded by that trigger. Name the trigger precisely.
- **G** knowledge/gotcha with no signature and no trigger beyond the pack's subject — stays prose (or the pack's skill).
- **H** requirement/product statement or platform setting mis-homed in a pack — re-home, do not convert.
- **X** already carried by an existing check/hook/test (name it) or made moot by the harness.

Be aggressive: "F with trigger X" or "B with set S" is a better answer than G whenever the moment of application or a static signature can be named, and prefer B over G for anything of the form "when you write X make sure Y exists/agrees elsewhere". Do not give up on a rule because it is hard; the point of this audit is to find what the mechanism must grow.

<result>Based on my comprehensive review of the official Claude Code documentation, here's the detailed answer to your questions about hooks and skills:

## Hooks and Skills Documentation Review

**URL Sources:** https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

---

1. **Complete hook event list and capabilities:**

The documented hook events are: `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`, and `Notification`. **Cannot verify in current docs:** `SubagentStop`, `PreCompact`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionRequest`, `ConfigChange`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCompleted`, `Elicitation`.

- **Can block (exit 2)?** Yes: `PreToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`  
- **Can inject context (`additionalContext`)?** Yes: `PreToolUse` and certain events per https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks ("JSON output format: `additionalContext`")

"Fires at three cadences: Once per session (`SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`), once per turn (`UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`), on every tool call (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse` except `EndConversation`)" (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).

---

2. **PreToolUse JSON output fields and input modification:**

Fields documented: `permissionDecision` (deny|allow), `permissionDecisionReason`, `additionalContext`. **Cannot confirm:** `updatedInput` field for modifying tool input. The docs show the output format but do **not** explicitly state whether PreToolUse can modify `tool_input`; this is **not verified in current docs**.

Input stdin carries: `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `tool_use_id` (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).

---

3. **UserPromptSubmit context and blocking:**

- **Can add context?** "Fires before Claude processes user prompt. Can block prompt." (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) — but specific JSON fields for context injection are **not documented**.
- **Can block?** Yes (exit 2).  
- **Stdin fields:** `session_id`, `prompt_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `permission_mode`, `hook_event_name`, `effort` per common input; **specific fields like `prompt text` are not itemized in current docs**.

---

4. **Matcher capabilities:**

- **MCP tools by name:** Yes. "MCP tools follow naming pattern `mcp__<server>__<tool>`" e.g. `"matcher": "mcp__memory__.*"` (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).
- **Bash by command content:** No direct confirmation; matchers are "match on tool name" for tool events per the reference. The `if` field gates by permission rule (e.g. `"Bash(rm *)"`) separately from the matcher.
- **Skill invocations:** **Not documented**. No matcher syntax shown for tool_name "Skill" with input matching the skill name.

---

5. **Hook `type`s:**

Documented types: `"command"`, `"http"`, `"mcp_tool"`, `"prompt"`, `"agent"` (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).

- **`prompt` type:** Yes — "LLM evaluation" with input `"prompt"` and `"model"` fields.  
- **`agent` type:** Yes — "Subagent-based verification" with `"prompt"` field.  
- **Which events support these:** "Prompt hooks" and "Agent hooks" documentation exists but **specific event compatibility is not itemized**.

---

6. **Skill/Plugin-scoped hooks:**

- **Skill frontmatter `hooks:` field:** **Not documented in current docs**. Skill frontmatter fields include `name`, `description`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `allowed-tools`, `disallowed-tools`, `context`, `agent`, `arguments`, `background`, `shell` (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills frontmatter reference), but **`hooks:` is not listed**.
- **Plugin `hooks/hooks.json`:** Mentioned as a hook location ("Plugin `hooks/hooks.json` — When plugin enabled"), but syntax/capability **not documented**.
- **Scope:** "Skill/Subagent frontmatter — Session scope" per hook locations table (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).

---

7. **Skill frontmatter fields:**

From https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills frontmatter reference:

Documented fields: `name`, `description`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `allowed-tools`, `disallowed-tools`, `context`, `agent`, `arguments`, `background`, `shell`. **`paths:` field is NOT documented for skills.** (Note: `paths:` exists for `.claude/rules/` files, not SKILL.md.)

---

8. **Path-specific rules in `.claude/rules/`:**

Path-specific rules **do exist**. From https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory:

"Rules can be scoped to specific files using YAML frontmatter with the `paths` field... Rules without a `paths` field are loaded unconditionally... Path-scoped rules trigger when Claude reads files matching the pattern, not on every tool use."

Pattern examples: `"src/api/**/*.ts"`, `"src/**/*"`.

---

9. **Stop hook stdin payload:**

Common fields: `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `permission_mode`, `hook_event_name`, `effort`. **Specific Stop-only fields like `stop_hook_active`, `last_assistant_message` are not itemized in docs**. Whether Stop can inject context into a continuing turn when it blocks is **not documented**.

---

10. **SubagentStop and hook inheritance:**

From https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents:

"Hooks from settings files, managed policy settings, and plugins all apply inside subagents... Subagent lifecycle events like `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop` fire when subagents start or finish."

Hooks in **skill/subagent frontmatter run only when that specific subagent is active**. Session-wide hooks (in settings.json) **do apply to subagents**.

---

11. **Hook mechanism for skill invocation:**

No documented hook event fires specifically on skill invocation/completion. The `Skill` tool itself has no special PreToolUse/PostToolUse handling documented. **This capability is not verified in current docs.** If a PreToolUse matcher `"Skill"` works, the skill name would need to come from `tool_input` parsing, which is **not documented**.

---

**Summary of unverified/missing items:**
- PreToolUse `updatedInput` field capability  
- UserPromptSubmit specific JSON schema  
- Bash command-content matching (only tool-name matchers documented)  
- Skill invocation hook mechanism  
- Skill frontmatter `hooks:` field  
- Plugin `hooks/hooks.json` detailed syntax  
- Stop hook payload beyond common fields  
- Which events support prompt/agent hook types</result>

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

################ packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/RULES.md ################
     1	# claudinite-fleet-sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
     2	
     3	## Configuring the fleet
     4	
     5	- **Keeping a repo out of the fleet** — add its full `owner/name` to `exclude` on this pack's
     6	  config entry. Nothing else opts a repo out: an archived or forked repo is reported as out of scope
     7	  but still walked, and a repo that simply never adopted is `uncovered`, which is a finding rather
     8	  than a choice. If a repo should not be measured, say so in `exclude` and the reports stop asking
     9	  about it.
    10	
    11	- **Adding or changing a `packSeeds` entry** — get it right *before* the sweep next runs. The
    12	  sweep seeds and never overrides, so a wrong seed reaches each member exactly once and then sticks;
    13	  correcting it here un-writes nothing, and undoing it is a change in every member's repo. Land the
    14	  entry and its own declaration together, then read the next run's report rather than assuming.
    15	
    16	- **Declaring a pack this fleet also seeds** — write the same config in both places, spelling
    17	  every default out on both sides rather than leaving one implicit. `seeds-agree` compares them
    18	  literally, because nothing in this pack may know what one pack's absent key means. A pack the
    19	  fleet standardizes on but this repo does not itself run has nothing to agree with, and is fine.
    20	
    21	## Acting on what a sweep reports
    22	
    23	- **Acting on an `add-packs` work-list issue** — the work is a declaration and a reviewed PR **in
    24	  the named member**, never here. A session in this repo is scoped to this repo, so if every item
    25	  names another repo there is nothing here to do: say the scope is the blocker rather than writing
    26	  to the issues, which are the only thing within reach and are not the work.
    27	
    28	- **Acting on a scanned pack suggestion** — it is a recommendation, never a verdict.
    29	  A fingerprint is a way to *suspect* a pack is wanted; whether to declare it is the member's call,
    30	  and closing the issue `not planned` is a standing answer the scan honours rather than re-opening.
    31	  A **forced** addition is the other thing entirely — a decision already made — so adopt what
    32	  its issue says instead of re-judging whether it was wanted.
    33	
    34	- **Reading `unknown` in a report** — it means the sweep could not look, not that it looked and
    35	  found nothing. Never convert one into a verdict: a repo whose declaration could not be read is
    36	  neither covered nor uncovered, an undecided fingerprint is not a non-match, and a member the
    37	  pack-seed sweep could not reach is not converged. Fix the access and re-run.
    38	
    39	- **Judging whether a member is behind** — compare `engineVersion` and `packVersions` against
    40	  canon, never the age of its stamped `ref`. The update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref` or
    41	  `updated`, so the stamp is provenance — which commit first vendored the mount — and stays
    42	  frozen on a member that is perfectly current. Its age measures nothing, and measuring it
    43	  calls the whole fleet behind on one arbitrary day.
    44	
    45	- **Answering why the fleet did not move** — read the member's own artifacts first: its
    46	  declaration, its stamp, the runs on its head sha. This repo dispatches; each member converges
    47	  itself, with its own token and its own delivery policy. Propose a settings change as a conclusion,
    48	  never as the diagnosis.
    49	
    50	## Running the manual levers
    51	
    52	- **Pushing canon to the whole fleet now** — create the work item, from a checkout of this repo:
    53	
    54	  ```
    55	  node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/create-work-item.mjs claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline
    56	  ```
    57	
    58	  Add `--context "REPOS=owner/a owner/b"` to narrow it (space-separated: a Context line splits on
    59	  commas), `--context "DRY_RUN=true"` to see the list without dispatching, or
    60	  `--context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"` to reach members that stopped their own scheduler on purpose.
    61	  Both knobs are read from the item's Context and nowhere else — an item created without them runs
    62	  unscoped and live. It queues one run per member and then FOLLOWS each to canon's published engine
    63	  and pack versions, reporting per member whether it converged, was already current, or never got
    64	  there — never a count of accepted dispatches. A member with nothing to do reads `already-current`,
    65	  which is a success, so over-using it is wasteful rather than unsafe.
    66	
    67	- **Adding a pack across the fleet** — create a `fleet-add-missing-packs` item with
    68	  `--context "ADD_PACKS=…"` rather than editing anything. No pack is named anywhere in this pack's
    69	  code: every id comes from config or from the item's own Context, which is what keeps the
    70	  enforcer from becoming a second place packs are known.
    71	
    72	## Credentials
    73	
    74	- **Granting or repairing `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`** — a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's
    75	  repositories, granted exactly what [`fleet-token.mjs`](fleet-token.mjs)'s table names — the only
    76	  place the permissions are written, because a per-sweep subset is always a defensible answer and
    77	  never the right one. Grant it whole: the token is granted once, for the pack.
    78	
    79	- **A sweep reporting `403` or `no-permission`** — the grant is short a permission, which the
    80	  error names. It is a grant to fix once, so widen the token rather than re-running: no sweep
    81	  retries, because a work list nobody will act on is not a green outcome.

################ packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md ################
     1	# core — working with Claudinite itself
     2	
     3	- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
     4	  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
     5	  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.
     6	
     7	- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
     8	  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
     9	  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
    10	  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
    11	  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
    12	  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.
    13	
    14	- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
    15	  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
    16	  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.
    17	
    18	- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
    19	  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.
    20	
    21	- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.
    22	
    23	- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
    24	  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
    25	  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
    26	  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.
    27	
    28	- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
    29	  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
    30	  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
    31	  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.
    32	
    33	- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
    34	  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
    35	  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.

################ packs/claudinite-growth/RULES.md ################
     1	# claudinite-growth — authoring Claudinite content here
     2	
     3	- **Recording a local pack change** — automatic work writes no changelog file there: the commit
     4	  and its PR are the record. A local pack is neither versioned nor distributed, so such a file
     5	  only aggregates unrelated changes into one line several runs a day contend for. A shared canon
     6	  pack still gets its `VERSIONS.md` row, which is what tells a member what a bump shipped.
     7	
     8	- **Wanting a job to run in Actions** — make it a task with a `code_work` command rather than
     9	  authoring a workflow; the vendored workflows already own the trigger, the concurrency, the
    10	  secrets and the failure reporting. Work with no cadence is a task too, on
    11	  `frequency: 'manual'`, woken by whatever knows the event happened.

################ packs/claude-code-web-users-support/RULES.md ################
     1	# claude-code-web-users-support — working from Claude Code on the web
     2	
     3	- **A person asking to change one of their personal preferences** — edit their `<email>.md` in the
     4	  preferences store repo this pack names, never here and never in the canon; a project convention
     5	  in disguise belongs in the pack owning its subject, and a preference triggering a command owns
     6	  only the trigger phrase.
     7	
     8	- **A person asking to record their personal preferences with no file yet** — create it in that
     9	  store repo, named for their exact identity plus `.md`, case included: the reader opens
    10	  `<path>/<email>.md` and nothing else, so any other name is silently never read.
    11	
    12	- **A web session halt-gated on a missing toolchain requirement** — re-paste
    13	  [`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh) whole and unedited into the
    14	  environment's Setup script field, then rebuild; a project-specific step belongs in its own
    15	  pack's `env` declaration, never in that body.

# store-release

## Why the declaration reads as it does

Carried over from the declaration's comments when it became `task.json`.

chrome-extension task: store-release — the pack-contributed release
trigger (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §6). STRUCTURAL Stage 2: `model: 'none'`
means the whole decision is code and there is NO agent phase —
the executor runs `worker.mjs` as code-work. This task ABSORBS the
release workflow's own independent 00:30 cron: the workflow becomes push +
workflow_dispatch only, and this task is the one place that fires its daily
leg, so the scheduler stays the repo's only cron (DESIGN §3, decision §11.6).

The whole contract is this default export; the unreleased-bump condition it
names lives in preconditions.mjs beside it.
Either an unreleased manifest bump (preconditions.mjs beside this file), or a
substantive change the dispatched workflow can diff shipped files against.
Ship-path precision is deliberately NOT re-derived here: the daily workflow
does the authoritative shipped-file diff against the latest release tag and
no-ops when nothing shippable moved, so this is the cheap pre-filter and the
workflow is the exact gate.

A repo that carries this pack but does NOT ship the Chrome Web Store pipeline
has no daily workflow for this task to fire. That is a fact adoption settled,
not a question worth re-asking nightly: such a repo names
`chrome-extension/store-release` in its `taskScheduler.disabledTasks`.

3:description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
30:- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
31:- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
33:- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
36:- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
39:- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
42:- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. 3:description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
30:- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
31:- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.

const hasHook = (value) =>
  (typeof value === 'string' && value.trim())
  || (Array.isArray(value) && value.some((c) => typeof c === 'string' && c.trim()));

const rule = {
  id: 'firebase/functions-predeploy-build',
  severity: 'blocking',
  description: 'A Firebase functions codebase with a build script wires that build as a firebase.json predeploy hook',
  doc: 'packs/firebase/RULES.md',
  why: 'without the hook a deploy ships whatever compiled output happens to be on disk — a local `firebase deploy` after an edit silently publishes the previous build',

  run(ctx) {
    const out = [];
    for (const { configFile, entry, source, manifest } of functionsCodebases(ctx)) {
      if (!manifest.scripts?.build) continue;
      if (hasHook(entry.predeploy)) continue;
      out.push(finding(rule, {
        file: configFile,
        what: `the "${source}" functions codebase declares a build script but no predeploy hook`,
        fix: `add "predeploy": ["npm --prefix ${source} run build"] to that functions entry in ${configFile}`,
      }));
    }
    return out;
  },
};

# ast-grep YAML Configuration Reference

## `rule`
"The object specify the method to find matching AST nodes." Rules operate on individual AST nodes within files during scanning.

## `constraints`
"Additional meta variables pattern to filter matches." Constraints are "applied after `rule`" — ast-grep matches the rule first, then filters results using constraints on single meta variables (not multiple ones like `$$$ARGS`).

## `utils`
"A dictionary of utility rules that can be used in `matches` locally." These reusable rule definitions are scoped to the current YAML rule configuration.

## `transform`
"A dictionary to manipulate meta-variables." Transformations process captured variables through operations like replace, enabling derived variable creation.

## `fix`
"A pattern or a `FixConfig` object to auto fix the issue." Fix patterns can reference captured meta-variables and may use empty strings to delete matched content.

## `files`/`ignores`
"`files`" applies rules only to matching patterns; "`ignores`" excludes matching patterns. The process: ignores are tested first, then files (if configured), otherwise all files are included by default.

First the callback `on_new_investigation` is called; if a cop needs to do its own processing of the AST or depends on something else. Then callbacks like `on_def`, `on_send` (see AST::Traversal) are called with their respective nodes. Finally the callback `on_investigation_end` is called."

## Key Callback Methods

**on_new_investigation:**
"Called before all on_... have been called. When refining this method, always call `super`"

**on_investigation_end:**
"Called after all on_... have been called. When refining this method, always call `super`"

## State Management Constraints

An important limitation states: "Between calls to `on_new_investigation` and `on_investigation_end`, the result of `processed_source` will remain constant. You should invalidate any caches that depend on the current `processed_source` in the `on_new_investigation` callback."

Additionally, the documentation notes that if a cop performs autocorrections, "your instance may be called multiple times with the same `processed_source.path` but different content."

# Key Concepts from OPA's Rego Policy Language

## Rules and Virtual Documents

"Rules define the content of virtual documents in OPA. When OPA evaluates a rule, OPA _generates_ the content of the document that is defined by the rule."

## Partial Rules with "Contains"

Rules generating sets use the `contains` keyword for incremental definitions: "instances contains instance if { ... }" allows multiple rules to contribute values to the same set document.

## Referencing Other Rules

Rules can reference other rules within the same package or imported packages. For instance, a rule might check "prod_servers[server]" to verify if a server exists in another rule's output.

## Quantifiers: Some and Every

The `some` keyword declares free variables for existential quantification: "some site in sites" checks whether a solution exists matching the constraint.

The `every` keyword expresses universal constraints: "every server in site.servers { endswith(server.name, '-dev') }" asserts the body holds for all domain elements.

## Recursion Limitation

An important constraint exists: **Rego does not support recursive definitions**. Rules cannot call themselves directly or indirectly, preventing infinite loops in policy evaluation.

# ESLint's Architectural Limitations for Type-Aware Linting

## Native Concept Statement

The maintainer stated: "ESLint today does not have any native concepts of cross-file dependencies, stateful parsing, or type information."

## Referenced ESLint Issues

**eslint/eslint#14139 (early 2021):**
A proposal was filed for an API permitting plugins to perform initialization work upfront. Brad provided extensive documentation regarding how type-aware linting functioned and what implementation would be necessary. The issue closed in 2025 without substantial discussion.

**eslint/rfcs#102 (late 2022–early 2023):**
This RFC requested information required for optimization of cross-file linting systems. Like its predecessors, it was closed with the intention of addressing concerns within a larger architectural redesign.

Both issues highlighted that ESLint's current design treats parsers as stateless functions, preventing them from understanding execution context—such as concurrent mode operation or session type—which is essential for efficient type-aware linting.

Based on the documentation provided, here's what it says about the `src` option and scanning:

**On the `src` option:**
"an array with files/paths to be analyzed. It only applies to unused exports. Defaults to `process.cwd()`, if not provided"

**Important caveat:**
The documentation does not explicitly address performance concerns or state that the rule's results depend on which files are passed to ESLint. However, the functionality description indicates the tool analyzes a defined set of source files to identify exports that lack static usage "within other modules in the same project," suggesting the analysis scope is limited to files you specify or configure.

But It Comes at a Cost. | by Anees Mehdi | Apr, 2026 | Medium","url":"https://medium.com/@aneesulmehdi/rego-is-good-but-it-comes-at-a-cost-09a17e1b1f91"},{"title":"Arbitrary recursion using dynamic data references · Issue #1565 · open-policy-agent/opa","url":"https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa/issues/1565"},{"title":"rego-recursion-error | Styra Documentation","url":"https://docs.styra.com/opa/category/rego-recursion-error"},{"title":"Recursion or transitive closure use case: supergroups · Issue #947 · open-policy-agent/opa","url":"https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa/issues/947"},{"title":"OPA Errors Guide | Open Policy Agent","url":"https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/errors"},{"title":"DEV Community","url":"https://dev.to/snyk/rego-for-beginners-part-2-combining-queries-with-andor-and-custom-messages-3bmp"}]

Based on the search results, here's what you need to know about recursive rules in Rego and OPA:

## Why Recursion Isn't Supported

An important property of Rego compared to general purpose programming languages is that policy evaluation should be known to terminate. Some common programming constructs, like while loops, or recursive references, can't reasonably provide such guarantees, and are therefore not allowed in Rego.

## When the Error Occurs

Recursion errors in Rego happen when a rule (or function, which is a special type of rule) makes a reference to either itself, or another rule that references the rule that made the original reference.

## Workarounds

If you need to handle recursive logic, there are alternatives:

1. **Precomputation**: A simple workaround could be to simply avoid recursion and instead write, say, a Python script that precompute all the transitive closure of the recursive part — all direct members and indirect members via group membership. Store the result as flat JSON and provide it to OPA as data.

2. **Unroll recursion**: It's often possible to "unroll" recursion for at least some depth... but if you need to support unbounded recursion, Rego is probably not the right language for the use case.

## Technical Limitation

It is a known boundary in logic: first-order logic cannot express graph reachability over arbitrary depth. Rego, without recursion, is essentially first-order logic over structured data.

# Semgrep Rule Syntax: Key Operators

**pattern-inside:**
"The `pattern-inside` operator keeps matched findings that reside within its expression. This is useful for finding code within other pieces of code, such as functions or if blocks."

**patterns (logical AND):**
"The `patterns` operator performs a logical `AND` operation on one or more child patterns. This is useful for chaining multiple patterns together where all patterns must be true."

**Metavariable Binding in patterns:**
"Metavariable values must be identical across sub-patterns when performing logical AND operations with the `patterns` operator." This ensures consistent variable matching across multiple conditions.

**metavariable-pattern:**
"The `metavariable-pattern` operator matches metavariables with a pattern formula. This is useful for filtering results based on a metavariable's value." It supports nested patterns and can specify target languages for string content analysis.

**metavariable-regex:**
"The `metavariable-regex` operator searches metavariables for a PCRE2 regular expression. This is useful for filtering results based on a metavariable's value." Matching is left-anchored by default.

**focus-metavariable:**
"The `focus-metavariable` operator focuses on, or _zooms in_ on, the code region matched by a single metavariable or a list of metavariables." It narrows match scope without performing new pattern matching itself.

content.content:
# ArchUnit Rule Structure

According to the documentation, architectural rules in ArchUnit follow a fundamental pattern. The guide states that "most architectural rules take the form: classes that ${PREDICATE} should ${CONDITION}."

The 'that' clause filters imported classes to a relevant subset, while the 'should' clause evaluates a condition against each selected class. When `rule.check(importedClasses)` is invoked, it evaluates all matched classes and generates an `AssertionError` reporting any violations with precise details like class names and line numbers.

## Code Example

Here's a practical illustration from the documentation:

```java
ArchRule rule = ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses()
    .that().resideInAPackage("..service..")
    .should().accessClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..controller..");

rule.check(importedClasses);
```

When this rule fails, the error message includes the complete rule description, violation count, and specific method calls causing violations. Developers can enhance clarity using `.because()` to document the rationale or `.as()` to replace the entire rule description.

content.content:
# Join Mode Overview

Join mode is an experimental Semgrep feature that runs multiple rules simultaneously and filters results based on cross-rule conditions. Here are the key aspects:

## What It Does

"Join mode runs several Semgrep rules at once and only returns results if certain conditions on the results are met." This allows detection of vulnerabilities that span multiple files by correlating findings across rules.

## How Rules Are Referenced

Rules are organized under `refs`, where each rule receives an identifier. As the documentation explains: "The `as` key behaves similarly to `AS` clauses in SQL. This lets you rename the result set for use in the conditions."

Example structure:
```yaml
refs:
  - rule: user-input.yaml
    as: user-input
  - rule: unsafe-template.yaml
    as: unsafe-template
```

## Joining Conditions

Conditions connect metavariables across rules using comparison operators:
```yaml
on:
  - 'user-input.$VAR == unsafe-template.$VALUE'
  - 'unsafe-template.$PATH > template-vars.path'
```

The `==` operator matches exact content equality, while `>` and `<` handle substring matching for file paths.

## Key Limitations

Join mode has significant constraints: it requires login and "does not work in the Semgrep Playground or Semgrep Editor, as it is an experimental feature." Additionally, "join mode only reports the code location of the **last finding that matches the conditions**," potentially obscuring earlier relevant matches. The feature is "not taint mode," meaning it may produce false positives when unrelated variables coincidentally share values.

content.content:
# Taint Mode in Semgrep

**Core Concept:**
Taint mode enables dataflow analysis to track untrusted data. As the documentation states: "Taint analysis is a dataflow analysis that tracks the flow of untrusted, or **tainted**, data throughout the body of a function or method."

**Key Components:**
Taint rules use four main operators defined in YAML:

1. **pattern-sources** (required) - identifies origins of tainted data
2. **pattern-sinks** (optional) - vulnerable functions where taint should not reach
3. **pattern-sanitizers** (optional) - operations that remove taint
4. **pattern-propagators** (Pro feature) - defines how taint spreads through code

A finding occurs when tainted data originating from a source flows to a sink without being sanitized.

**Analysis Scope:**
The documentation notes an important distinction in capabilities: "Using the CLI option `--pro-intrafile` when invoking Semgrep, Semgrep performs interprocedural (across functions), _intra_-file (within one file) analysis." Meanwhile, the Pro engine with `--pro` enables cross-file analysis for supported languages. Community/OSS versions perform intraprocedural (within-function) analysis, while Pro extends tracking across function and file boundaries.

No, this page does not list join mode as deprecated. 

The page documents three deprecated experiments:

1. **Equivalences** - "This feature was deprecated in Semgrep v0.61.0."
2. **Extract mode** - "As of Semgrep 1.65.0, extract mode has been deprecated and removed from Semgrep."
3. **Turbo Mode** - "As of June 16th, 2025, Turbo Mode has been deprecated and removed from the Semgrep Playground."

Join mode is not mentioned anywhere on this page.

# Analysis of Semgrep's Analysis Types

Based on the documentation provided, here are the key distinctions:

**OSS/Community Engine Limitation:**
"By design, Semgrep open source software, Semgrep Community Edition (CE), can only analyze interactions within a single function, also known as **intraprocedural analysis**."

**Pro Engine Capabilities:**
"Semgrep Code runs **cross-function (interprocedural)** analysis by default, and gives security teams the option to trade off speed for better results and deeper analysis with **cross-file analysis**."

**Cross-File Analysis Definition:**
"Cross-file analysis finds patterns spanning multiple files within a project to help security engineers deeply understand their organization's security issues."

**Cross-Function Analysis Definition:**
"Cross-function analysis finds patterns within a single file spanning code blocks and functions."

**Key Difference:**
"By analyzing interactions across files and functions, Semgrep Code can reduce noise, uncover new vulnerabilities, and make results easier to understand."

The documentation does not explicitly mention "taint tracking across files" in the provided content. The focus is on pattern detection spanning files and functions rather than specific taint-tracking methodology.

content.content:
# Recursive Joins in Semgrep

Recursive joins enable Semgrep to follow chains of matches transitively across a codebase. The feature uses the `-->` operator to construct recursive queries that build chains like function calls or class inheritance.

## Key Features

"Recursive join mode has a recursive operator, `-->`, which executes a recursive query on the given condition." This allows rules to approximate callgraphs by recursively joining tables with themselves, matching transitive relationships not directly present in the source code.

## Syntax Example

```yaml
on:
  - 'callgraph.$CALLER --> callgraph.$CALLEE'
  - 'user-input.$SINK == callgraph.$CALLER'
```

The `-->` operator chains metavariables recursively, generating all transitive paths through matched patterns.

## Limitations

"Join mode only works on the metavariable contents, which means it's fundamentally operating with text strings and not code constructs." This creates potential for false positives when similarly-named metavariables are extracted across different contexts, since the matching operates on text rather than semantic code analysis.

# Multi-pass (collect-then-assert) designs in lint and static-analysis tools

**Sourcing note.** This sandbox's egress proxy blocks the canonical doc hosts (eslint.org, typescript-eslint.io, semgrep.dev, codeql.github.com, souffle-lang.github.io, ast-grep.github.io, rustc-dev-guide, pylint.readthedocs.io, docs.rubocop.org, archunit.org, conftest.dev, openpolicyagent.org). Every claim below was instead read from the **source repository of the same documentation on github.com** (or pkg.go.dev), and the URL cited is the one actually fetched. No claim rests on search snippets alone, except where marked *(snippet)*. A human with an unblocked browser can re-verify against the canonical hosts; a later agent pass here cannot.

## 1. ESLint

**Per-file collect-then-report.** A rule's `create()` returns visitor callbacks; a key ending in `:exit` "calls that visitor function while going **up** the tree", so `Program:exit` fires after the whole file was walked — the idiomatic place to report over state accumulated in the closure during descent. — https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/main/docs/src/extend/custom-rules.md

**`--fix` multi-pass loop.** "After applying fixes, ESLint will run all the enabled rules again on the fixed code, potentially applying more fixes. This process will repeat up to 10 times, or until no more fixable problems are found." (same doc). The bound is `const MAX_AUTOFIX_PASSES = 10;` — https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/main/lib/linter/linter.js

**Why rules are single-file.** typescript-eslint's maintainers: "ESLint today does not have any native concepts of cross-file dependencies, stateful parsing, or type information." — https://github.com/typescript-eslint/typescript-eslint/discussions/11568. The request for a first-class "Plugin initialization API" (project-wide setup before per-file linting) was closed as not planned — https://github.com/eslint/eslint/issues/14139.

**Workarounds.** typescript-eslint typed linting: "This requires TypeScript to analyze your entire project instead of just the file being linted", at "the performance penalty of asking TypeScript to do a build of your project before ESLint can do its linting" — the TS `Program` is a de-facto first pass — https://github.com/typescript-eslint/typescript-eslint/blob/main/docs/getting-started/Typed_Linting.mdx. eslint-plugin-import builds its own cross-file view: "Memoization is used at various levels to avoid the copious amount of `fs.statSync`/module parse calls" (https://github.com/import-js/eslint-plugin-import), and `no-unused-modules` takes a `src` option, "an array with files/paths to be analyzed … Defaults to `process.cwd()`", i.e. the rule scans the project itself rather than relying on ESLint's file set — https://github.com/import-js/eslint-plugin-import/blob/main/docs/rules/no-unused-modules.md

## 2. Semgrep

**Metavariable binding.** `patterns` is a logical AND and "Metavariable values must be identical across sub-patterns"; `pattern-inside` "keeps matched findings that reside within its expression"; `metavariable-pattern` "matches metavariables with a pattern formula"; `focus-metavariable` "zooms in on the code region matched by a single metavariable". Within one rule this is a join on the metavariable name, scoped to one file. — https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep-docs/blob/main/docs/writing-rules/rule-syntax.mdx

**Join mode (cross-rule, cross-file).** "Join mode runs several Semgrep rules at once and only returns results if certain conditions on the results are met." Sub-rules are named under `refs` (`as` "behaves similarly to `AS` clauses in SQL") and `on` conditions equate metavariables across them (`user-input.$VAR == unsafe-template.$VALUE`; `>`/`<` are substring tests used for paths). Caveats: it "only reports the code location of the **last finding that matches the conditions**", and "only works on the metavariable contents, which means it's fundamentally operating with text strings and not code constructs". — https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep-docs/blob/main/docs/writing-rules/experiments/join-mode/overview.mdx. A recursive operator exists: "`-->` … executes a recursive query on the given condition", e.g. `callgraph.$CALLER --> callgraph.$CALLEE` to approximate a call graph — https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep-docs/blob/main/docs/writing-rules/experiments/join-mode/recursive-joins.mdx. Join mode is still marked experimental and is not on the deprecated list — https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep-docs/blob/main/docs/writing-rules/experiments/deprecated-experiments.mdx

**Taint mode as derived facts.** "Taint analysis is a dataflow analysis that tracks the flow of untrusted, or **tainted**, data throughout the body of a function or method"; `pattern-sources`, `pattern-sinks`, `pattern-sanitizers`, `pattern-propagators` each yield a set of matches, and the finding is the derived relation *source reaches sink unsanitized*. Scope: CE "can only analyze interactions within a single function (intraprocedural)"; `--pro-intrafile` is "interprocedural (across functions), *intra*-file", and `--pro` adds cross-file. — https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep-docs/blob/main/docs/writing-rules/data-flow/taint-mode/overview.mdx and https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep-docs/blob/main/docs/semgrep-code/semgrep-pro-engine-intro.mdx

## 3. CodeQL / Datalog engines

"To create a database, CodeQL first extracts a single relational representation of each source file in the codebase"; then "one or more queries are executed against it … written in … QL" — extraction and querying are two separate products. — https://github.com/github/codeql/blob/main/docs/codeql/codeql-overview/about-codeql.rst. "Strictly speaking, a predicate evaluates to a set of tuples", and predicates are the named intermediate results shared by queries — https://github.com/github/codeql/blob/main/docs/codeql/ql-language-reference/predicates.rst.
